#9546. This Breakfast Addition Sharpens Memory Later In The Day

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

A simple breakfast addition improved reaction times, but its effects on memory took a more complicated turn.

Adding walnuts to breakfast could help people respond faster on mental tasks and learn information more effectively later in the day.

A generous handful produced small cognitive benefits over the following six hours, although memory performance varied with the timing of the tests.

Walnuts may influence how the brain directs attention and obtains the energy needed for demanding mental work.

Professor Claire Williams, study co-author, said:

“A handful of walnuts with breakfast could give young adults a mental edge when they need to perform at the top of their game.”

The research involved over 30 healthy young adults aged 18–30, who ate two different breakfasts on separate visits to the laboratory.

One contained 50 g of crushed walnuts mixed into muesli and vanilla yoghurt, while the other contained no nuts.

The breakfasts contained almost identical calorie and fat totals, with butter added to the comparison meal to help achieve this match.

Participants completed tests before breakfast and again two, four and six hours afterwards, while researchers also recorded their brain activity.

After the walnut breakfast, participants responded faster on tasks involving attention, resisting distractions and switching between different mental rules.

These abilities form part of executive function, which helps us control our responses and adapt to changing demands.

The differences were modest, averaging around eight milliseconds on the attention test and 22 milliseconds when switching between rules.

Whether improvements of this size would make a noticeable difference outside the laboratory remains uncertain.

The memory findings were more complicated.

Two hours after eating walnuts, participants performed slightly worse when repeatedly learning and recalling a list of words.

By six hours, however, the pattern had reversed, with better performance after walnuts than after the comparison breakfast.

One possibility is that walnuts helped protect learning performance as the testing day wore on.

Repeated mental effort can make it harder to take in new information, so preserving the ability to learn could be useful even without improving every aspect of memory.

However, participants did not report feeling less mentally fatigued after walnuts, leaving this explanation unconfirmed.

Another possibility is that some benefits emerged gradually as nutrients were absorbed and processed.

Walnuts contain omega-3 fats, protein and plant compounds called polyphenols, which could contribute individually or together.

Electrical recordings revealed differences in frontal and parietal brain activity after the two breakfasts.

These regions contribute to attention, memory and the control of behaviour.

The changes may indicate that walnuts altered how mental resources were allocated during the tests, although they do not establish precisely why performance improved.

Blood samples also showed slightly higher glucose availability and lower concentrations of circulating free fatty acids after walnuts.

Greater glucose availability might help fuel demanding mental work.

The study was published in the journal Food & Function (Bell et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9545. Charles Dickens’s writing chalet and Hastings Castle added to list of English heritage sites at risk

Left: Charles Dickens' Writing Chalet, Rochester, Kent. Right: Hastings Castle

Dickens’ chalet: Photo: Nick Johnson - The Imageworks. Hastings Castle: © Historic England Archive

The cabin where Charles Dickens spent the last day of his life, the home in Stratford-upon-Avon of William Shakespeare’s daughter Susanna and the castle built by William the Conqueror high on the cliffs above the town of Hastings are among 197 buildings and sites added to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register today (5 November).

The list identifies sites such as buildings, parks, battlefields and shipwrecks that are threatened by decay, neglect or inappropriate development. There are now 4,991 entries on the register, all of which are labelled as of national importance. This encompasses 197 sites that were added this year.

The miniature Swiss chalet which became the writing retreat of Charles Dickens was a Christmas gift to the author in 1864, arrived flat packed in 94 pieces, and was put together by a theatre carpenter after Dickens and his house guests failed. Dickens placed it at the furthest end of the garden, reached by a tunnel he built under the road at his last home, Gad’s Hill, near Rochester in Kent. He spent much of 9 June 1870 working in the chalet on The Mystery of Edwin Drood, before returning to the house where he died that night, aged just 58.The house, now a school, and tunnel survive, but the chalet was moved in the 1960s to the garden of Eastgate House in Rochester, where it is now too fragile for public access.

Hall’s Croft, an imposing timber-framed building dating from 1613, was the home of Susanna Shakespeare and her husband John Hall. After many uses, and residents including the playwright George Bernard Shaw and the bestselling Victorian romantic novelist Marie Corelli, it was acquired by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust and opened to the public in 1951. It had already been closed for several years for extensive conservation work when, in October 2025, a car reversed into the facade and caused further serious damage. The playwright Ken Ludwig has donated £1m to the work but major fundraising will still be needed.

Hall’s Croft, Old Town, Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire

Hastings Castle was one of the first three such sites built by William the Conqueror after his victory in the famous battle—and is depicted in the Bayeux Tapestry. The site, with a sweeping view across a stretch of the coast, has a long history, with remains of an Iron Age fort having been discovered there. The castle’s commanding site has made it very vulnerable to storms and coastal erosion and there have already been urgent works to stabilise its ruins. Future plans for the site include the creation of a new visitor centre and cafe.

Along with the sites that have been added this year there is good news: 85 sites for which solutions have been found, and which have now been removed from the register. They include the storm-lashed Newlyn Harbour in Cornwall and a little hut in the Gloucestershire garden of Edward Jenner, in which, in 1796, he performed the first-ever vaccinations.

A pair of elegant Georgian houses in east London, built around 1715 and Grade II* listed, had an unusual saviour: Tottenham Hotspur Football Club, which has converted them—with help from the Lottery Heritage Fund—into artists studios, gallery spaces, and a cafe. The space is run by Sarabande Foundation, which was founded by the late fashion designer Lee Alexander McQueen.

The Georgian terraced house saved from dereliction by Tottenham Hotspur FC. The house is now home to artists’ studios, galleries and café run by Sarabande Foundation, which was established by Lee Alexander McQueen

Rescue grants available include the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund and the Places of Worship Renewal Fund, both funded by the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and administered by Historic England, and the Countryside Stewardship Heritage Service.

The UK’s heritage minister Baroness Twycross said in a statement that the register has a crucial role in identifying historic places in need of support. “Every part of the UK is bursting with history, so it is vital we protect the heritage sites at the heart of communities which help tell the stories of our nation.”

Claudia Kenyatta and Emma Squire, the joint chief executives of Historic England, said the most effective way of protecting the sites was to bring them back into use.“The sites saved and removed from the Register this year show what can be achieved when partners and communities work together to deliver positive lasting change.”

#9544. How to stop nightmares and fall back asleep after bad dreams

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, CDCES, MBA

Nightmares can be really tough. They jolt us awake in the middle of the night, often in a cold sweat with a racing heart, and the residue of the bad dream leaves us feeling shaken and on edge, making it hard to fall back asleep. And we all know how much more challenging everything else becomes when our sleep is disrupted.

Recurring nightmares can wreck your sleep and leave you feeling drained, anxious, or unsettled the next day. If you’ve found yourself googling, “why do I keep having nightmares?” or, “how to stop bad dreams every night,” you’re not alone.

Nightmares can be triggered by everything from stress and sleep disorders to late-night snacks or certain medications. Thankfully, there are proven strategies to reduce their frequency and help you get back to sleep after a bad dream.

Let’s explore common nightmare causes, tips to prevent them, and techniques to calm your mind and body when you wake up in the middle of the night.

Sleep disruptions, like frequent nightmares and bad dreams, can take their toll on our well-being. It’s not just about feeling tired the next day. It’s about how those disturbances affect our mood, energy levels, productivity, and our mental health. Getting enough sleep is crucial when it comes to rejuvenating our bodies and resting our minds, but when you’re experiencing nightmares on the reg, peaceful sleep can feel like a distant dream.

But there is hope. With awareness and understanding of what’s causing your nightmares, along with some effective strategies, it’s possible to manage, if not prevent, bad dreams. Tools such as mindfulness and meditation can help you cultivate a more peaceful mind and significantly improve the quality of your sleep.

Nightmares don’t tend to be random. They’re usually the product of various factors at work in our subconscious or conscious minds. So a key factor in tackling nightmares is being able to understand what’s prompting them.

Stress and/or anxiety: Perhaps unsurprisingly, frequent nightmares can be the product of stress or anxiety that’s present in our waking life. It’s like your mind extends the day’s worries into your sleep. That upcoming work presentation, conflict with your partner, or just the sheer weight of day-to-day tasks can all find their way into your dreams, causing nightmares.

Eating too close to bedtime: That late-night snack might be more trouble than it’s worth. And no, it’s not just cheese, which, by the way, doesn’t actually cause nightmares. Heavy or spicy meals, in particular, can lead to physical discomfort that disturbs your sleep, often inducing vivid and sometimes bad dreams.

Scary movies, TV shows, or books: Love a good horror movie or thriller book before bed? You might want to rethink that. Your subconscious can weave elements of the contents of whatever you’ve been reading or watching into your dreams, creating some pretty unsettling mental visualizations when the lights go off.

Traumatic experiences: If you’ve been through a particularly challenging event either recently or in the past, the trauma of whatever happened could show up in your dreams. This is normal. It’s your brain’s way of processing the trauma, but it can lead to recurring nightmares, which can be distressing and even prevent sleep.

Alcohol, drugs, and/or caffeine: It may feel like alcohol and drugs ease you into sleep more easily than going to bed unassisted, but these substances often disrupt the quality of your sleep and can lead to vivid, intense nightmares.

Medications: Some prescription drugs, including certain types of antidepressants, blood pressure medicines, and beta blockers, can lead to bad dreams. If you’ve started a new medication and are experiencing frequent nightmares, you might want to talk to your doctor.

Sleep disorders: Sleep conditions like sleep apnea and restless leg syndrome can disrupt sleep and lead to nightmares. If you’re experiencing symptoms such as daytime sleepiness or morning headaches, please check in with a healthcare provider.

Knowing what triggers your nightmares is the first step in gaining control over them. Remember, the goal isn’t to eliminate all dreams but to cultivate a more relaxed sleep experience. After all, dreams are a natural part of sleep, and many of them can be magical, rejuvenating, and creative experiences.

Now that we know what might be causing nightmares, here are some strategies to help keep bad dreams at bay.

Routines aren’t just for kids, and the value of a consistent sleep schedule can’t be overstated. Your body thrives on routine, so a regular sleep and wake time helps your body understand when it’s time to wind down and when it’s time to rise.

Consider your sleeping environment. Is it dark, quiet, and cool? These are ideal conditions for restful sleep. Also, consider investing in a comfortable mattress and pillows. These small changes can significantly impact your sleep quality and help prevent bad dreams.

If stress or anxiety is the culprit behind your nightmares, it’s important to tackle the cause head-on. Implementing stress management techniques, such as deep breathing exercises or guided mindfulness practices (such as this one), can work wonders in soothing your mind before bed.

Try to wind down at least an hour before bed. This means turning off the TV, stepping away from work, and switching off any other devices. This quiet time allows your mind to transition smoothly into sleep mode.

Regular physical activity can promote better sleep, helping to prevent nightmares. Just ensure you don’t exercise too close to bedtime, as it can have the opposite effect.

As mentioned before, late-night snacking, especially heavy or very spicy food, can lead to bad dreams. Finish eating at least a few hours before hitting the hay.

Incorporate relaxing activities into your bedtime routine. This could include reading, listening to relaxing music, or practicing mindfulness exercises. It’s all about calming your mind and preparing your body for sleep.

If something’s bothering you, don’t let it stew in your mind. Talking it out with a trusted friend, family member, or professional can help release some of the burden.

Both these substances can disrupt your sleep cycle and might increase the likelihood of having nightmares. Try limiting them or avoiding them altogether.

If you suspect your medication is causing nightmares, discuss it with your healthcare provider. They might be able to adjust the dosage or suggest alternatives.

Implementing these strategies can make a big difference in preventing nightmares and improving the overall quality of your sleep. Everyone deserves a good night’s sleep, and you’re no exception. Remember, it’s not about perfection but progress, so celebrate small victories and keep experimenting to find out what works best for you.

The biggest challenge after waking up from a nightmare is often trying to calm your body and mind enough so you can get back to sleep. If you’ve ever found yourself wide awake at 3 a.m., staring at the ceiling, you know exactly what we’re talking about.

So how exactly do you drift back into the land of nod once you’ve been rudely awakened by a nightmare? Here are seven strategies that might help you fall back asleep after a bad dream.

Deep, controlled breathing can be a powerful tool in helping to calm your mind and body. The practice works by shifting your focus away from any disturbing images from your nightmare and redirects it onto the rise and fall of your breath. An easy-to-follow technique is the 4-7-8 breathing method, where you inhale for 4 counts, hold your breath for 7 counts, and exhale for 8 counts.

This technique involves tensing and then releasing different muscle groups in your body. Start from your toes and work up to your head (or vice versa). This can help you feel more grounded and take your mind off the images or content of your nightmare.

Picture a peaceful, calming scene. It could be a beautiful beach, a serene forest, or any place that brings you joy and tranquility. Focusing on images that make you feel relaxed and at ease can steer your mind away from whatever you were dreaming about.

If you’re finding it hard to fall back asleep, get out of bed and do something relaxing. This could be reading a book, listening to calm music, or doing a low-intensity activity like drawing. Do whatever feels soothing to you, and try to do it somewhere quiet and in low-lighting so your body can ease into relaxation and sleep. If in doubt, try listening to a Sleep Story.

If you wake up scared, turning on a soft, gentle light can feel comforting. In some ways, it feels like you’re banishing the darkness from your dream, and being able to see your surroundings makes you feel safer and more at ease. Just make sure its not too bright or it may, ironically, end up disrupting your sleep.

Writing down whatever happened in your nightmare can be therapeutic. In some ways, the process of writing helps to drain away the power the bad dream has over your emotions. Keep a notebook and pen beside your bed and if a nightmare wakes you up, write it down. Here’s a Dream Journal you can download and print out.

If you’ve been startled awake by a nightmare, take a moment to center yourself. Notice your surroundings, the feeling of the sheets, the sounds you can hear. This can bring you back to reality and help separate the images of your nightmare from the safety of your bedroom. Repeat to yourself: “I am here. I am safe.”

Finding it difficult to fall back to sleep after a nightmare is perfectly normal. Don’t pressure yourself to get back to sleep immediately. Take your time, be gentle with yourself, and use the techniques above to help guide your mind and body back into a state of ease.

Here at Calm, we’re committed to helping you cultivate a more peaceful state of mind during your waking hours and as you journey through the world of sleep.

Nightmares can be triggered by a variety of factors. Common triggers include stress or anxiety, late-night eating, exposure to disturbing content like horror films or books, traumatic experiences, substance use like alcohol or drugs, certain medications, and sleep disorders.

Similar to the triggers mentioned above, these factors can cause nightmares. Preventing nightmares often involves addressing these underlying causes. This could mean establishing a healthy sleep routine, creating a sleep-friendly environment, managing stress, avoiding stimulating activities before bed, exercising regularly, avoiding heavy meals before bedtime, and talking about what’s troubling you. Remember that everyone’s different, and what works best for you might differ from what works best for others.

While occasional nightmares are normal, having them every night is not typical and can be distressing. Frequent nightmares can interfere with your sleep quality and overall well-being. If you’re experiencing nightmares regularly, speaking to a healthcare provider or a mental health professional may be beneficial to identify any underlying issues that might need addressing.

Yes, many people experience nightmares less frequently as they age. However, some adults do continue to have nightmares. Addressing the underlying causes of nightmares, like stress or anxiety, can significantly reduce their frequency. Remember, occasional bad dreams are normal, but if they are causing significant distress or affecting your sleep, it’s worth discussing this with a healthcare provider.

Nightmares can be challenging, but understanding their triggers and implementing strategies to manage them can help you reclaim a peaceful night’s sleep.

Frequent nightmares can be caused by high stress levels, anxiety disorders, PTSD, sleep disorders like sleep apnea, or even certain medications. Alcohol and late-night eating can also disrupt REM sleep, where most nightmares occur. If they persist nightly, it might be worth speaking to a medical or mental health professional.

To break the cycle of nightly nightmares, focus on improving sleep hygiene—stick to a consistent sleep schedule, avoid screens and heavy meals before bed, and create a calming wind-down routine. You might also consider meditation or breathing exercises before bed. If the nightmares are rooted in trauma, therapy like CBT-I or imagery rehearsal therapy may help.

Yes, certain medications can help reduce the frequency and intensity of nightmares, especially in cases linked to PTSD or anxiety. Prazosin, for example, is sometimes prescribed off-label for this purpose. Always talk to your doctor before considering medication for sleep-related issues.

Nightmares activate the body’s stress response, which can jolt you out of sleep with increased heart rate and adrenaline. If you wake up after a bad dream, grounding exercises like deep breathing or progressive muscle relaxation can help you calm down and return to sleep more easily.

Fear of sleep after a nightmare is common. Your body may still be on alert, so lying down can feel unsafe.

Start by slowing your breathing and naming a few things you can see in the room. A soft light is fine if it helps you feel safe. You don’t have to fall asleep right away. Sitting up with a book in low light until you feel calm is okay, and dropping the pressure to sleep often eases the fear.

If the fear comes back the next night, keep your bedtime routine the same and avoid replaying the dream in your head. Writing it down earlier in the day can help. Fear that keeps returning, or frequent nightmares, is worth raising with a doctor or mental health professional.

Bad dreams (nightmares) happen during REM sleep and usually involve vivid, disturbing scenarios that you remember upon waking. Night terrors occur during non-REM sleep and involve sudden arousals, often with screaming or thrashing, but the person usually doesn’t remember them. Night terrors are more common in children but can affect adults too.

Nightmares are difficult. But help getting back to sleep after a bad dream is easy. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9542. Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth

Many important choices seem to pit reason against emotion. Popular culture often describes that tension as a contest between two parts of the brain: a newer, more advanced center for rational thought and an ancient "lizard brain" that runs on instinct.

But the evolutionary history of the brain appears to be far more complicated than a simple struggle between old and new.

"There was a theory proposed in the '50s that the brain evolved in layers starting with basic bodily functions, to emotions in the reptilian brain, leading up to sophisticated reasoning in humans," explains Nabil Imam, an assistant professor in the School of Computational Science and Engineering and a faculty member with Georgia Tech's Institute for Neuroscience, Neurotechnology, and Society (INNS). "This is not how an evolutionary biologist would think about the problem."

Research published in Science Advances suggests that brain evolution may be better understood in terms of wiring rather than newer regions being stacked on top of older ones.

By examining the organization of both biological brains and artificial neural networks, Imam and his colleagues found evidence that evolution may involve allocating a limited amount of brain space among competing wiring strategies. Their model describes a computational tug of war between two fundamentally different kinds of neural organization, both of which are established even before birth.

The findings could help explain a long-running puzzle in brain evolution and may also point toward new ways of building AI systems that use less data and energy.

Terms such as "logical brain" and "lizard brain" actually refer to groups of brain regions with very different functions. The neocortex, often associated with higher-level thought, forms the outer layer of the brain and is involved in vision, perception, reasoning, and other complex abilities.

The so-called lizard brain is harder to define so neatly.

"The limbic system, sometimes called the 'reptilian brain,' controls emotion broadly speaking -- but it also has other components with distinct functions," explains Imam. The system contains separate regions involved in memory, smell, navigation, and emotional regulation. "Why do people group all these different regions into one big system? There hasn't been a good theory for what is common between these different circuits."

To explore that question, the researchers compared how these brain systems change across species. Rather than looking at individual regions one at a time, they examined how the limbic system and neocortex vary together over evolutionary history.

A clear pattern emerged. When one part of the limbic system was relatively large, the other limbic regions also tended to be larger. At the same time, the neocortex was generally smaller.

That suggests the regions are not evolving independently.

"Rather," says Imam, "it's a coordinated expansion of these regions across species."

The pattern points to the limbic system behaving more like an integrated network than a collection of unrelated structures. Across evolution, its different components appear to expand and contract together.

The next question was what might cause that coordinated shift.

Imam's explanation centers on the way different brain systems are wired before birth.

Neural circuits in the neocortex are arranged as spatial maps. Brain regions that process nearby parts of the body, such as the thumb and index finger, are also located near one another. Similar spatial organization appears in systems that handle sight and sound.

The limbic system is organized differently. Instead of being laid out spatially, its wiring works more like a bar code, with distributed patterns of activity representing particular smells or complex memories.

The researchers used AI models to test whether these differences arise from built-in architecture or are mainly learned through experience.

When an AI network was created with localized, spatial connections, it was naturally well suited to processing vision, sound, and touch. In contrast, distributed "barcode-style" networks were necessary for strong performance on smell recognition and memory.

An Evolutionary Competition for Brain Space

The researchers then investigated why the relative size of these brain systems changes so consistently among species.

The basic idea is that the brain has limited resources. Space and energy are finite, so natural selection may favor whichever wiring system is most useful for survival in a particular environment.

To test this, the team created a multimodal artificial network in which spatial and distributed systems competed for "real estate."

When the simulated environment rewarded smell, every region within the distributed system expanded while the neocortex became smaller. When vision was favored instead, the pattern reversed.

This trade-off may help explain striking differences between real animals. The nine-banded armadillo, which depends heavily on smell, has a very large limbic system. The squirrel monkey, which relies strongly on vision, has a brain dominated by the neocortex.

Across the 182 species included in the study, the findings suggest that brain evolution is less about adding progressively newer layers of "logic" and more about shifting space between different wiring systems according to what helps an animal survive.

The same principle may have implications beyond biology.

If engineers can reproduce some of this built-in neural organization in artificial intelligence, they may be able to create systems that learn more like biological brains and require far less training data and energy.

"Today's artificial neural networks are trained by vast amounts [of] data -- it's about nurture," says Imam. "But the brain is not a blank slate that gets trained by experience. It is a mix of nature and nurture, and the nature is that pre-wired architecture."

"We could translate that architecture to AI systems to make it more brain-like, or make it learn or function as efficiently as the brain."

This work was a collaboration with Cornell University and was supported by the National Science Foundation.

Materials provided by Georgia Tech. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9540. How to be more productive: 6 tips to help you get things done

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You start your day with a plan: clear your to-do list, get ahead, maybe even sign off early. Instead, your attention gets pulled in every direction. Back-to-back calls, a stream of emails, countless tabs open at once. Next thing you know, the day's almost over, your list is still full, and you're left wondering how you’re supposed to get anything done.

Busyness and productivity can look identical from the outside, but they’re not the same. You can stay busy all day tackling small, urgent-feeling tasks without ever touching the work that really counts. Being productive means doing the tasks that matter, which requires staying intentional about where your time and energy go.

So what's getting in the way of your productivity, and what can you do about it? Here’s a closer look at the everyday friction that can slow you down, plus a few shifts to help you make the most of each day.

Most productivity drains are minor, routine points of friction that are easy to miss, yet they add up fast. A few usual suspects:

Context switching: Research shows that every jump between tasks costs you the time it takes to mentally reset, even when it feels instant.

Constant interruptions: Responding to notifications and drop-in requests can feel productive, but it turns your attention to other people's priorities.

Unclear priorities: When everything feels urgent, you often default to whatever's quickest instead of what matters most.

Running on empty: Skipping breaks seems like it saves time, but it slows you down later and wears down your focus.

Procrastination: When a task feels overwhelming or unclear, it’s tempting to reach for something more manageable instead of starting the job you need to do.

Good news: you can reduce these points of friction without turning your whole day upside down. The tips below aren’t a set system, just a few ideas you can implement on your own terms. Start with one or two, and notice what feels different.

Decide what would make today count before you open your inbox. Not five things, just one that matters most. Write it down somewhere visible, then dedicate the first stretch of your day to that task before anything else pulls your focus away.

💙 Start your day mindfully with this Finding Focus practice on Calm.

Multitasking may feel efficient, but your brain can’t really do two things at once. It's switching fast between them, and each switch costs you a little focus and energy. Over a full day, those costs add up.

Try working in single-task blocks. Close the extra tabs, silence your phone, and stay with one task until it's done or you hit a natural stopping point. You'll often finish faster than if you’d juggled three tasks at once.

💙 Learn more with Jay Shetty’s Settle Down by Single-Tasking session on Calm.

The apps and platforms you use are built to stretch your attention in a dozen directions. Every ping invites you to switch tasks, and you’re driven to take the bait without thinking twice.

You don't have to go off-grid to take back control. Check your email at two or three set times instead of leaving it open. Turn off notifications you don't need, and put your phone in another room during focused work. If one site keeps tempting you, a browser blocker can hold the line.

💙 Explore Digital Distractions from the 7 Days of Focus series on Calm.

Your focus isn't a tap you can leave running. If you push too long without pausing, your attention frays, mistakes creep in, and even small tasks can start to feel hard.

Try working in stretches of about 25 minutes, then step away to stretch, breathe, or look out a window. It’s also worth protecting your downtime in the evenings and on weekends, so you're not completely drained by mid-week.

💙 Dr. Alex Pang makes the case for smarter rest in The Power of Rest, a Calm masterclass.

Your to-do list is probably a mix of very different kinds of work. A report needs deep focus. A stack of emails or calls may not need any. Some work requires creativity, while some mainly requires attention to detail. Tackling tasks in a random order means starting cold, over and over.

But if you batch similar tasks, you can move through them while you're already warmed up for that type of work. Keep your quick replies to a couple of set windows instead of scattered across the day, and stack your calls so they run one after another. Once you're in the groove of one kind of work, staying there beats starting over.

A task tends to stretch to fill whatever time you give it. Timeboxing flips that. You pick a task, decide up front how long it gets—say 30 minutes—then stop when the time runs out, whether you're finished or not. That cap keeps one email from swallowing a whole morning, and stops you from polishing something long past the point of diminishing returns.

It also takes the guesswork out of what comes next, since you've chosen in advance. Block the slot on your calendar and set a timer. When the box closes, decide consciously whether the task gets another round.

💙 If starting is the hardest part, these 9 techniques can help you stop procrastinating.

You can train yourself to be more productive by gradually incorporating new helpful habits, like choosing a top priority for the day, single-tasking, and reducing digital distractions. Start with one small change and repeat it until it feels natural. One well-known study found that a new behavior took an average of 66 days to feel automatic—ranging from 18–254 days depending on the person—so give yourself time to adjust.

Yes, people with ADHD often struggle with productivity, and it’s not about effort or willpower. ADHD involves differences in executive function, the mental skills you use to start tasks, plan, and hold attention. This is why even starting tasks you want to do can feel difficult. The strategies in this article are still useful, though you may need to adapt them to what works for your brain.

💙 If ADHD is getting in the way of your work, here’s more on why that happens and how to deal with it.

Productivity peacocking is when you put more energy into looking busy than into doing meaningful work. Think replying to messages instantly instead of finishing the task at hand, or reorganizing your to-do list for the third time instead of crossing items off.

There's no single best time of day to work, since it depends on your body clock and when your energy naturally rises. Instead of trying to follow someone else's schedule, notice when you feel most alert, and dedicate that window to your most demanding work.

Yes, it's possible to be more productive without working longer hours, since a lot of time gets lost to switching tasks and reacting to interruptions. Try protecting focused blocks, sticking to one task at a time, and taking proper breaks, since a tired brain works slowly and rest can help you get more done.

Stress affects productivity by making it harder to focus, plan, and think clearly. When you're stressed, your brain pulls resources away from the areas that handle focus and memory. Bring your stress down and calm your mind with a few minutes of slow breathing.

One of the most effective ways to stop getting distracted while working is to remove the distraction before you start. Silence notifications, close the extra tabs, and place your phone out of reach so you're not relying on willpower in the moment. When your mind wanders anyway, and it will, bring it back without giving yourself a hard time.

Yes, meditation can help you be more productive, though the effect is indirect. In one randomized study, a two-week mindfulness course improved people's working memory and reduced how often their minds wandered mid-task.

You don't need long sessions, and even a few minutes a day of focusing your attention on your breath works the same mental muscle you use to stay on track while working.

#9539. HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month

Using an in-home HEPA purifier for one month spurs a small but significant improvement in brain function in adults age 40 and older. That’s the result of a new study we co-authored in the journal Scientific Reports.

HEPA purifiers – HEPA stands for high efficiency particulate air – remove particulate matter from the air. Exposure to particulate matter has been connected to respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses as well as neurological diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s. Environmental health researchers increasingly recommend that people use HEPA air purifiers in their homes to lower their exposure to particulate matter, but few studies have examined whether using them boosts mental function.

We analyzed data from a study of 119 people ages 30 to 74 living in Somerville, Massachusetts. Somerville sits along Interstate 93 and Route 28, two major highways, resulting in relatively high levels of traffic-related air pollution. This makes it an especially good location for testing the health effects of air purifiers.

We randomly assigned participants to one of two groups. One used a HEPA air purifier for one month and then a sham air purifier – which looked and acted like the real thing but did not contain the air-cleaning filter – for one month, with a monthlong break in between. The second group used the real and sham purifiers in reverse order.

After each month, participants took a test that measured different aspects of their mental capacity. The test probed people’s visual memory and motor speed skills by measuring how quickly they could draw lines between sequential numbers, and it tested executive function and mental flexibility by asking them to draw lines between alternating sequential numbers and letters.

We found that participants 40 years and older – about 42% of our sample – on average completed the section testing for mental flexibility and executive function 12% faster after using the HEPA purifier than after using the sham purifier. That was true even when we accounted for factors like differences in the amount of time participants spent indoors, with either filter, as well as how stressful they found the test.

This improvement may seem small, but it is similar to the cognitive benefits that people experience from increasing their daily exercise. While you may not experience a sudden increase in clarity from a 12% boost, preventing cognitive decline is vital for long-term well-being. Even small decreases in cognitive functioning may be associated with a higher risk of death.

Air pollution can negatively affect mental function after just a few hours of exposure. Studies show that air purifiers are effective at reducing particulates, but it’s unclear whether these reductions can prevent cognitive harm from ongoing pollution sources like traffic. Research has been especially lacking in people living near major sources of air pollution, such as highways.

People living near highways or major roadways are exposed to more air pollution and also experience higher rates of air pollution-related diseases. These risks aren’t encountered by all Americans equally: People of color and low-income people are more likely to live near highways or areas with heavy traffic.

Our study shows that HEPA air purifiers may offer meaningful health benefits under these circumstances.

Research shows that air pollution begins to affect cognitive function especially strongly around age 40. These effects may become increasingly prominent as people age.

HEPA air purifiers may therefore be especially beneficial for older adults. Our study did not explore this possibility, as fewer than 10 of our 119 participants were over the age of 60.

Also, our participants only used a HEPA air purifier for one month. It’s possible that longer durations of air purification may sustain or even increase the improvement in cognitive function we observed in our study.

Finally, it is unclear exactly how air purifiers improve cognition. Some studies suggest that exposure to particulate matter reduces the amount of the brain’s white matter, which helps brain cells conduct electrical signals and maintains connections between brain regions. The brain regions most harmed by air pollution are the ones that control mental flexibility and executive function, the same domains in which we saw improvements in our study.

We plan to study whether reducing particulate matter by using air purifiers is indeed protecting the brain’s white matter, and whether it could reverse some cognitive decline. We will explore that possibility by studying how levels of molecules called metabolites, which cells produce as they do their jobs, change in response to breathing polluted air and air cleaned by a HEPA filter.

#9538. What is languishing? Meaning, signs, and how to cope

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Mental health struggles aren’t always obvious to the people experiencing them. Sometimes, you might just feel… stuck. You’re not exactly sad, but you’re not happy either. You’re not falling apart, but you’re definitely not thriving. That feeling is called languishing, and it’s more common than you think.

Basically, languishing is the state of mind between depression and flourishing. It’s that foggy middle ground where life feels muted.

And while languishing might not seem like a big deal, if you ignore it, it can quietly erode your sense of joy and purpose. That’s why it’s so important to understand what languishing is and explore ways to lift the fog and feel more connected to yourself again.

Languishing is the emotional equivalent of treading water. You’re not drowning, but you’re not moving forward either. You’re just floating, tired, and maybe even a little numb.

On the mental health spectrum, languishing falls somewhere between depression and flourishing — and it can come on so subtly that you don’t even realize it’s happening. If you’re languishing, you might struggle to concentrate or feel “meh” more days than not. You might not be able to remember the last time something excited you, or just have a general feeling of going through the motions without any real sense of meaning.

And because languishing doesn’t always feel like a problem that needs solving, it can be easy to ignore. Don’t. If it’s left unchecked, languishing can lead to deeper mental health challenges over time.

Languishing may seem similar to depression, burnout, and anxiety, but they’re different in key ways. Here’s how:

Depression: Depression is usually deeper and heavier than languishing. It can include persistent sadness, hopelessness, and a loss of pleasure in everything. You may also feel disconnected from yourself or others in a way that requires clinical care.

Burnout: Typically, burnout comes from chronic stress. It leads to emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and a sense of being overwhelmed. Languishing can overlap with burnout, but it’s usually broader, affecting your energy in all areas of life.

Anxiety: Anxiety is often high-energy and fear-based. It can show up as worry, racing thoughts, or a sense of dread. On the other hand, languishing feels flat.

Languishing can slowly build, dulling your emotional energy. Here are some reasons why it happens:

Chronic stress: Nonstop work pressure or caregiving can wear down your nervous system.

Disconnection: Not feeling connected to meaning can make your life feel empty or purposeless.

Prolonged uncertainty: Global unrest or personal instability can leave you emotionally worn out.

Lack of novelty: Doing the same thing day after day can cause your brain to check out from boredom.

Isolation: Lack of meaningful interactions can make you feel unseen or untethered.

If you’ve been feeling off without knowing why, you could be experiencing languishing. Here are five signs:

You’re coasting: You’re showing up and ticking boxes, but it all feels mechanical. You feel disconnected from any real sense of drive or direction.

Flow feels out of reach: Things you used to lose yourself in, like reading, creating, laughing, and dancing, have lost their appeal. You’re finding it hard to immerse yourself in anything, no matter how meaningful it once felt.

Your motivation has disappeared: Small plans you used to get excited about—like a weekend walk or trying a new recipe—now feel like uphill climbs. It takes more effort, and there’s less satisfaction.

Your emotions feel muted: You’re not experiencing intense sadness necessarily, but you’re also not feeling much else. It’s also harder to feel joy and excitement when things are going well.

Time feels strange: Days feel like they blend together, and you feel like you’re in a fog.

Languishing can make it hard to change things up and rebuild. But all change, no matter how big or small, starts with just one step. That’s all you have to do — one teeny step at a time.

Here are 10 small but meaningful ways to slowly begin moving forward.

Saying “I think I’m languishing” can bring a surprising sense of relief. It creates space between you and the experience.

It tells you that you’re not lazy, broken, or dramatic. You’re just in a tough emotional patch. Naming it gives you power, and it reminds you that this is a state, not a character flaw.

Read more: 10 mindfulness questions to help you check in with yourself

When you’re languishing, trying to feel great can backfire. Your goal should be to reconnect with anything that feels nourishing—like a song or a hot shower—not to feel endlessly inspired.

Start with where you are and slowly shift your internal goalposts from “thriving” to “engaged enough to care again.”

Here are 10 ways to reconnect with yourself if you’re feeling off right now.

Flow is that magical zone where you’re so absorbed in something that time disappears. You don’t have to lose hours. Just five to 10 minutes of doing something immersive can help to light you up again.

Try cooking a familiar recipe while listening to music or watering your plants, and notice how they’ve changed. You could also play a game on your phone that feels satisfying.

💙 Listening to Flow with Tamara Levitt can help you find yours.

Rigid routines can feel impossible when you’re low on energy, but a little structure helps.

Anchoring yourself with a morning stretch, a mid-day walk around the block, or a journaling session before bed might be just what you need to start feeling more like yourself.

Read more: 6 best morning stretches to wake up & start the day right

We tend to isolate when we’re languishing, but connection, even in tiny doses, can be one of the most effective antidotes. Consider sending a “thinking of you” message to someone you love or exchanging a friendly “hello” with your local barista.

Refocusing your attention can make you feel more centered.

Try turning off your phone while you eat a meal, reading a book for 10 minutes straight, or even concentrating on one movie instead of flipping between shows.

Get back into a hobby, a place, or a type of music you used to love. It may not be inspiring right away, and that’s okay. Many times, the action leads to the emotion.

Simple, restorative movement can help shift your mental energy, even subtly.

Try stretching in bed before you get up, doing a few yoga poses, or just taking your next phone call while standing.

💙 Get your blood pumping during this Mindful Movement session with Mel Mah.

Good enough is fine. Eat the frozen meal, ignore the dishes, or wear the same sweatshirt two days in a row. You don’t have to be impressive. You just have to be kind to yourself. Here are 10 ways to cultivate more self-kindness in your life.

You’re allowed not to be okay. If that’s the case, consider reaching out to a professional to see if they can help you get to the root cause of your emotions.

If asking for help feels too hard, try reaching out to a trusted friend. You could simply start by saying, “Hey, I’m not doing great. Can we talk soon?” or “I’m feeling off lately, and I just need someone to listen.”

Tiredness typically has a clear cause—like maybe you didn’t sleep well—and once you rest, the tiredness goes away. On the other hand, languishing persists even after you get some sleep or take time off.

Unlike simple exhaustion, languishing is an emotional and mental dullness that makes everything feel like a chore. If you’re waking up after a full night’s rest and still feeling apathetic or disconnected, you could be languishing.

There isn’t an official test for languishing, because it isn’t a clinical diagnosis. Researchers use a 14-question survey, developed by sociologist Corey Keyes, to sort people into languishing, moderate, or flourishing mental health. It’s built for research, so it can’t diagnose you.

Have most days felt flat or foggy for weeks?

Is it hard to feel interested in things you used to enjoy?

Does the feeling stay even after you rest?

If you said yes to several, you may be languishing. If you’re unsure, a doctor or mental health professional can help.

Languishing isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but that doesn’t mean it’s not real or important. Languishing is what psychologists call a “subclinical” state. This means that it doesn’t meet the criteria for mental illness, but it’s still a sign that your mental health needs attention.

Languishing is your brain’s version of a check engine light. It’s telling you that something’s off.

Languishing and depression can feel alike, so look at how heavy the feeling is and how it affects your days. When you’re languishing, you can usually keep up with daily life, but everything feels flat or foggy.

Depression goes deeper. It often brings hopelessness or feelings of worthlessness, and it can make daily tasks like working or sleeping hard.

If your mood is getting heavier, hasn’t lifted in several weeks, or you feel hopeless, talk to a doctor or mental health professional. If you can’t tell which one you’re dealing with, that’s reason enough to ask. Mindfulness can help with languishing, but it’s not a replacement for care.

Languishing isn’t another word for an existential crisis, but they can overlap. An existential crisis usually involves questioning the meaning of life, your purpose, or your place in the world. It tends to be philosophical and emotionally intense.

On the other hand, languishing is more like emotional white noise. Instead of asking, “What’s the point of it all?” You tend to ask,  “Why don’t I care about anything right now?”

That said, languishing can often trigger bigger questions about meaning and direction, especially if it lingers.

Languishing can last anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on your circumstances and support system. Sometimes it can fade on its own, especially if your environment changes or if you start naturally reconnecting with things that bring you energy. But often, it sticks around until you intervene.

If you’d like to stop feeling this way, small shifts in connection, movement, attention, and routine can start to turn the tide. The key is to treat it seriously, even if it feels subtle, because you deserve to feel alive again.

#9537. Rare Altdorfer landscape previously unknown to scholars to be auctioned next month

Albrecht Altdorfer, A thickly wooded landscape with a rainbow behind the trees and a distant outcrop to the right beneath a cloud-laden sky (around 1520)

A rare landscape by the German Renaissance artist Albrecht Altdorfer will be offered at auction at Sotheby’s Old Masters Evening Sale in London on 9 December, with an estimated price of between £3m and £5m.

The painting of a thickly wooded landscape and a rainbow against a densely clouded sky, dating from around 1520, surfaced in a Swiss private collection. It was previously unknown to Altdorfer scholars and does not feature in the artist’s catalogue raisonné. It is one of only three known oil landscapes by Altdorfer, who is considered one of the first landscape artists. The other two are both in museums—one is in Munich’s Alte Pinakothek, and the other in London’s National Gallery.

“To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field,” says George Gordon, the chairman of Sotheby’s Worldwide Old Masters Department.

The current owner of the painting inherited it from his father, who purchased it in 1957 from the collection of a noble Austrian family, the House of Harrach. Painted on parchment, it was later glued to a wooden panel support. It is the smallest of Altdorfer’s known landscapes. A distant castle perches on a rocky outcrop beyond the rain-wettened forest and undergrowth that dominates the painting, which is signed.

Altdorfer was born in 1480 in Regensburg in southern Germany, spent most of his career there, also working as a politician, and died in the city in 1538. His densely wooded landscapes are drawn from the mixed deciduous and evergreen forests either side of the Danube downstream from Regensburg, Gordon says.

He says it was difficult to give a price estimate for the painting because no Altdorfer work has been offered on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery paid the reported sum of £2.4m for Christ Taking Leave of His Mother (around 1520). It was one of the highest prices ever paid for a work of art at that time.

“We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon says. “It could fetch more than our estimate. I think it’s quite likely that museums will be interested.”

Sotheby’s will exhibit the painting in New York from 7-19 November and in London from 4-9 December.

#9536. Where is the best place to meditate? Here’s how to find your spot

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

You have a free morning and want to meditate, but you’re not sure where. The living room isn’t private or quiet enough. The lighting in your home office is harsh. In your bedroom, the only place to sit is your bed, and you’re worried you might fall asleep. So instead of practicing mindfulness, you end up weighing the risks of distraction or discomfort.

The good news is, you don't need a Pinterest-worthy space, just a spot that works for you. People practice on train platforms, in parked cars, and on office floors during their lunch break, and they still get the benefits.

Whether you're just getting started or you’ve been meditating for years, this guide will help you find and level up that spot.

A good meditation space is one where you feel safe, comfortable, and undisturbed. These four qualities tend to make the biggest difference:

Comfort: A supportive cushion, a chair with a good backrest, or even a spot against the wall reduces strain on your body.

Quiet: Minimal noise, foot traffic, or notifications helps you avoid competition for your attention.

Calming sensory cues: Soft lamplight, a candle, a diffuser, or a warm blanket can signal it’s time to slow down.

Familiarity: The same corner or cushion becomes a cue over time, so your brain starts to wind down as soon as you arrive.

💙 Just starting out? Here’s a detailed guide on how to meditate for beginners.

The best place to meditate depends on what you want from your session, and many people rotate between a few spots. Indoors is more predictable, since weather and temperature are rarely a factor. Outdoors, on the other hand, can feel more grounding and restorative.

When you meditate indoors, you have more control over the temperature, lighting, and setup of the space, which can help you build a consistent habit.

Your bedroom corner. It's private and may already feel like a place to recharge, so it works well when you want to slow down.

Your living room. This spot works best when it’s empty, like early morning before anyone's up or once the house has gone quiet for the night.

Your unused nook or closet. With just a cushion and a curtain, almost any small, overlooked area can become your own little sanctuary.

Your bed. Meditating here is a gentle way to start your day or transition into sleep, though the same comfort that makes it appealing can also make you doze off before you're done.

💙 For ways to turn any of these spots into a dedicated space, see Calm's meditation room ideas.

💙 For more on the bed option specifically, check out bedtime meditation techniques.

The outdoors offers something special: fresh air, the open sky, and nature sounds that help calm your nervous system. Time in green space is linked to lower cortisol and reduced stress. One explanation is the attention restoration theory — the idea that natural settings give your focus a chance to recover.

A backyard or garden. If you have one, some greenery and a comfortable seat can turn it into a peaceful retreat.

A beach or park. Either works especially well near water, where the sound of waves or a stream can ease your mind.

A balcony or patch of grass. Even a small outdoor space gives you a change of scenery, which can help you relax.

💙 For more on practicing outside, see Calm’s guides on outdoor meditation and building a meditation garden.

If sitting feels hard, try walking meditation. Focus on the rhythm of your steps to give your mind something to settle on.

A few small, deliberate changes can turn your meditation space into one that genuinely supports your practice.

Store your cushion, blanket, and anything else you use to meditate in your dedicated place. When you return to the same spot consistently, ideally around the same time, settling in can start to feel automatic.

Face away from clutter, toward a blank wall or window. In a shared space, a folding screen or blanket draped over a chair can mark off your corner. Even with your eyes closed, feeling tucked away can help you settle.

Try playing steady background noise—like soothing nature sounds or music—to cover unpredictable and intrusive sounds like traffic or a neighbor's TV. If you prefer some structure in your practice, you could follow a guided meditation.

To slow down, experiment with tracks around 60–80 beats per minute, which researchers have linked to a slower heart rate. For daytime focus, many people find that ambient or instrumental sound works best.

💙 Calm's guides on meditation music can help you find what fits your needs.

Put your phone on Do Not Disturb, and tell the people you live with that you'll be unavailable for the length of your session. You could also pick a time when they’re less likely to need you.

💙 Try the Single-Tasking session with Jay Shetty on Calm.

If you need to take the strain off your lower back, sit on a cushion or folded blanket to raise your hips slightly above your knees. You can also meditate near a wall, or place a chair nearby to support your spine if sitting upright gets tiring.

A meditation cushion can help you hold your position more comfortably. Try keeping the room on the cool side too, since an overly warm setup can nudge you toward sleep.

💙 Explore the Posture session from the 7 Days of Calm series.

💙 Learn about the different meditation postures to find the right fit for you.

Where you meditate shapes how the practice feels once you're there, but consistency is what matters most. A pleasant space can motivate you to start, though it's not required.

You can still meditate in a noisy home or busy neighborhood, and plenty of people do. Headphones with a guided session or ambient sound can add a bit of calm almost anywhere, even a parked car or a bathroom.

You can even let the noise become part of the practice by resting your attention on the sounds themselves, instead of trying to push them away. Over time, that flexibility often makes your practice stronger.

You don’t need much to set up a meditation corner. A cushion, a clear patch of floor, and some calming objects are enough. Pick an empty corner and mark it off with a plant, a small rug, or a curtain.

Meditating in bed is fine, and it's a gentle way to wind down at night or start your morning. If you’re worried about dozing off, sit up against the headboard instead of lying down, or try it earlier in the day when you’re more alert.

To reduce distractions when you meditate, start with what you can control: silence your phone and pick a time when interruptions are less likely.

For noises that still come up, treat your breath as your anchor and return to it whenever your mind wanders.

💙 Calm's guides on what to focus on during meditation and how to improve focus go deeper on taming a wandering mind.

Your meditation space doesn't need to look a certain way. It just needs to work for you. Soft light, minimal clutter, and something comfortable to sit on are usually enough.

Music and calming sounds can ease you into your meditation. Soft instrumental tracks, nature sounds, or steady background noise all help mask distracting noises and signal to your body that it’s time to relax.

As your practice develops, you might find you prefer silence, so it's worth experimenting to see what suits you.

#9535. Does ADHD Worsen With Age? It Depends.

Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first became meaningful to how sensitive one’s ADHD is to their environment.

Not too long ago, ADHD was largely thought of as a childhood condition that diminished in adulthood. Today, we understand that ADHD is a lifelong condition. What’s less clear: How does ADHD change across the lifespan, if at all?

This is a question that professor and clinical psychologist Margaret Sibley, Ph.D., addressed during her ADDitude webinar, “How ADHD Symptoms & Impairments Change with Age.”

The answer is still coming into focus but one central truth is emerging: There isn’t a single ADHD experience. Whether ADHD worsens or improves over time for someone depends on multiple factors, from when symptoms and impairments first become meaningful to how sensitive the individual’s ADHD is to their environment.

Sibley’s take-home from the research? “It depends on who you are.”

The question of how ADHD changes over time — whether it gets better or worse for people — is tricky, in part, because of the symptom vs. impairment question. That is, someone may show symptoms of ADHD, but the degree to which those symptoms impact their life may shift with age, overall health, and myriad other circumstances.

[Your Free Guide to ADHD in Older Adults]

“Not everyone who has symptoms is impaired,” Sibley said.

From major life transitions (like perimenopause and its accompanying impacts on cognition), environmental demands (e.g., a job that strains executive functioning) to coping skills, what’s going on in someone’s life “may influence whether a person actually experiences problems because of their symptoms,” Sibley said.

The question of whether ADHD worsens or improves over time suggests that the condition is linear. For many people, this is not the case.

“It doesn’t get better or get worse. But depending on what’s happening in your life, you may have good years and not-good years,” Sibley said, whose research found that higher environmental demands are associated with “better-functioning ADHD.”

[Read: ADHD’s Vanishing and Reappearing Act]

If you’ve experienced symptoms and impairments since childhood, your symptoms will likely get better, while impairments may or may not worsen.

If your symptoms first began to impact you in adulthood — perhaps triggered by aging, hormonal fluctuations, or other changes — research suggests that your symptoms and impairments may worsen over time.

If you’re part of the subgroup of people whose ADHD fluctuates from year to year, you may have a form of ADHD that is environmentally sensitive.

#9534. Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain

Before birth, the human brain is assembled through an enormous series of cellular choices. At the center of this process are radial glia, a special type of stem cell that helps create many of the features that distinguish the human brain.

These cells produce large numbers of the neurons and support cells that make up the cerebral cortex, the brain region involved in thought, memory, and language. Radial glia are also believed to contribute to the unusually large expansion of the human cortex compared with that of other species. Although most disappear before birth, similar cells can later appear again in brain cancers for reasons scientists still do not fully understand.

"Radial glia are the coolest cells that have ever existed," said Aparna Bhaduri, an assistant professor of biological chemistry at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. "They're really key to making us human. But they're also at the center of many neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders, as well as cancer -- so understanding how they make their decisions is one way to start understanding how those conditions arise."

Two new studies published in Cell and Science now provide a closer look at how radial glia make those developmental choices. Bhaduri and her colleagues found that the cells respond to two very different kinds of information: the way they process nutrients and direct physical signals from another part of the developing brain. Together, these findings offer new insight into how the human cortex produces its remarkable variety of cell types.

In the Cell study, researchers built a detailed map of metabolism in the developing human cortex. The project was a collaboration between Bhaduri's lab and Heather Christofk's lab and was led by co-first authors Jessenya Mil and Jose Soto.

To create the atlas, the team analyzed donated human tissue along with brain organoids grown from stem cells. Their results pointed to an unexpected conclusion: metabolism does not simply support brain development in the background. It can actively influence which kinds of cells are produced.

The researchers found that radial glia depend heavily on the pentose phosphate pathway, a metabolic process that uses glucose to make materials needed by cells that are dividing rapidly.

When the scientists lowered the amount of available glucose or interfered with this pathway, the stem cells changed what they produced. They began generating more inhibitory neurons and other cell types that normally appear later in development.

"What was surprising is that metabolism isn't just a passive thing that happens in the background," said Bhaduri, a member of both the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center. "It can really control how stem cells make decisions."

The results could help scientists investigate how maternal nutrition, metabolic disorders, and other environmental influences affect the developing brain. The metabolic atlas also provides one of the most detailed resources yet for researchers studying metabolism during human brain development.

The second study, published in Science and led by first author Claudia Nguyen, examined a completely different source of developmental information. This time, the researchers focused on signals coming from the thalamus, a structure deep inside the brain that helps relay information throughout the nervous system.

Scientists have known for years that neurons in the thalamus send long projections toward the cortex. These wire-like fibers eventually form connections with specific cortical neurons. However, anatomical studies have shown that in humans, the projections reach the cortex long before those final connections are established.

That raised an important question: Why do the fibers arrive so early?

Using human stem cell-derived brain "assembloids," the UCLA researchers found part of the answer. The thalamic projections physically touch radial glia while the brain is still developing.

That contact changed the behavior of the stem cells. It caused them to produce more excitatory neurons, the primary signal-carrying neurons in the cortex. The effect was especially strong for upper-layer neurons, which are particularly expanded in the human brain.

"We already knew that these projections influence how the cortex develops," Bhaduri said. "What we specifically found is that this influence comes through an actual physical connection between the projections and the radial glia -- a point of contact that just hasn't been identified before, and one that very likely does not exist in rodents."

A gene linked to autism enters the picture

The researchers connected this physical interaction to NRXN1, a gene already known for helping neurons form connections with one another. Mutations in NRXN1 have previously been associated with autism spectrum disorder.

To investigate its role, the team created assembloids from patient-derived cells carrying an NRXN1 mutation. In these models, the altered thalamic signals behaved differently from signals made by unaffected cells.

Those changes shifted the balance between the number of stem cells and the neurons they generated. The result offers researchers a possible way to study how disturbances early in brain development could influence the formation of the cortex.

The developing brain is in constant communication

Although the two studies focused on very different mechanisms, they point toward the same broader idea. One examined metabolism, while the other explored neural connections, yet both showed that radial glia do not make their decisions in isolation. Their behavior is continuously shaped by signals from the environment around them.

The studies also demonstrate how dramatically organoid technology has changed the study of human brain development. About a decade ago, scientists had few practical ways to directly investigate how uniquely human neural stem cells behave.

Today, brain organoids and related models allow researchers to recreate important features of human brain development in the laboratory. These systems also make it possible to test questions that cannot be addressed through animal models alone.

Bhaduri hopes the findings will encourage scientists to view metabolism and physical cellular connections as active drivers of development rather than as background processes.

"Ultimately, these studies give us a glimpse under the hood of how these cells make decisions," she said. "Understanding those decisions is a first step toward understanding normal brain development, disease vulnerability and, potentially, how similar stem-cell programs operate in brain cancer."

This research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, the National Science Foundation, the Brain & Behavior Research Foundation, the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Rose Hills Foundation, the Esther A. & Joseph Klingenstein Fund, the Simons Foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network, the International Foundation for Ethical Research, the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center's Stem Cell Research Training Program, and the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center and UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center Ablon Scholars Program.

#9533. What Happier People Tend To Believe About Others

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

A review involving over 2.5 million people links one social outlook to greater happiness—and the connection runs both ways.

Trusting others is linked to greater happiness and life satisfaction, a review involving over 2.5 million people finds.

Happier people also tend to become more trusting over time.

The link between trust and happiness is slightly stronger in children, adolescents and older adults, possibly because supportive relationships are especially important at these ages.

Trust may help meet the need to belong by making it easier to build relationships in which people feel supported and secure.

The research combined almost 1,000 findings from studies involving people aged six to 84.

The analysis examined how trust related to everyday emotions, including happiness and sadness, as well as people’s overall satisfaction with their lives.

Greater trust was consistently associated with better wellbeing.

The association was somewhat stronger among children and adolescents than among young and middle-aged adults, and stronger among older adults than young adults.

Trust may matter more at ages when people are building close relationships or becoming more dependent on others.

For younger people, learning whom to trust is part of building meaningful friendships and supportive social networks.

In later life, people may prioritise a smaller circle of close relationships and depend more on others for support.

The researchers distinguished between trust in familiar people, trust in people generally and trust in institutions.

The first involves confidence in someone known personally, such as a partner, friend or relative.

General trust involves expectations about people more broadly, including strangers, while institutional trust concerns organisations such as governments, banks and the police.

All three were associated with better wellbeing, but trust in familiar people showed the strongest connection.

Trust may support wellbeing partly because close relationships require a willingness to be vulnerable.

Expecting someone to respond with care can make it easier to seek help, cooperate and maintain a supportive connection.

These relationships may satisfy the basic psychological need to feel connected to others and cared for in return.

Trust could also provide a broader sense of security and predictability, making the social world feel more dependable.

This may help explain why trust was slightly more closely related to overall life satisfaction than to positive or negative emotions.

Life satisfaction reflects a broader assessment of how life is going, whereas emotions can fluctuate with immediate experiences.

The relationship also worked in the other direction, with greater wellbeing predicting more trust later.

One proposed explanation is that emotions influence how people interpret the world around them.

Feeling happy may encourage more positive perceptions of other people, while anxiety may draw attention towards threats and uncertainty.

Trust and wellbeing could therefore reinforce each other, with supportive expectations helping people feel better and positive feelings making trust easier.

The wider social environment mattered too, with a stronger connection between trust and wellbeing in countries where people were generally more trusting.

A trusting outlook may be more beneficial when the people around us are dependable.

Simply encouraging someone to trust more overlooks the behaviour of the people and institutions receiving that trust.

Professor Catrin Finkenauer, study co-author, said:

“But trust can’t be forced—it has to be earned.”

The findings therefore highlight the importance of honesty, reliability, transparency and fair treatment in relationships and institutions.

“When we build trust, we also support mental health and stronger communities.”

The study was published in the journal Psychological Bulletin (Bi et al., 2025).
