#9532. Do you have a fear of leaving the house? How to cope with agoraphobia

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Some days, even the thought of stepping outside can make your chest tighten. The world feels too big, too unpredictable, and your home feels like the only place that's safe. This experience is more common than most people realize, and it often points to something called agoraphobia, or the fear of leaving the house.

People who experience agoraphobia aren't necessarily weak, but rather trying to create safety and control in their day-to-day experience. This particular phobia can stem from intense experiences like trauma, but can also be rooted in genetics and lived experience. While there's nothing wrong with wanting to feel safe at home, agoraphobia can make everyday tasks like running errands or going to work feel daunting and overwhelming.

Learning to ease back into exploring the world at large can help make life feel more… well, livable. So, let's explore what causes agoraphobia, what can make it worse, and a few evidence-based ways to start rebuilding a sense of ease in the world and the return of your freedom.

Agoraphobia often starts with a negative experience. A panic attack on the subway, a dizzy spell in a grocery store, a sudden wave of fear that seems to come from nowhere. When that happens, the body remembers and starts building invisible boundaries to prevent it from happening again. What starts as caution can slowly turn into avoidance, until even ordinary outings feel overwhelming.

Clinically, agoraphobia is often linked to anxiety or panic disorders, though it can develop on its own. The fear isn't about the world itself, but about losing control or facing uncomfortable sensations in public. If you've ever thought, “What if I panic and can't escape?” that's the loop agoraphobia reinforces. And your brain's attempt to protect you ends up feeding the fear.

Past panic attacks or trauma: Experiences that felt unsafe or uncontrollable can leave the body on high alert long after the danger has passed.

Chronic stress or burnout: When your nervous system is constantly under strain, it becomes more reactive to triggers.

Family history or genetics: Anxiety disorders can run in families, likely due to a mix of inherited traits and learned coping patterns.

Personality and temperament: People who tend to be more sensitive, cautious, or introspective may notice and internalize physical sensations more deeply, which can heighten fear responses.

Other mental health conditions: Depression, social anxiety, and PTSD can all overlap with or contribute to agoraphobic symptoms.

Read more: What are the most common phobias? Plus, how to treat them

Agoraphobia doesn't always look the same for everyone. For some, it's a strong hesitation to go far from home. For others, it means avoiding specific situations where escape might feel difficult or embarrassing, like crowded stores, public transit, or open spaces. The fear isn't necessarily about the place itself, but about what might happen once you're there.

These symptoms can range from mild to severe and may come and go. You might still leave the house sometimes, but only under specific conditions, or you might find that even opening the door feels unbearable. Here are a few common symptoms:

Physical symptoms often overlap with panic or anxiety responses. You might notice:

A racing heartbeat, shortness of breath, or dizziness

Feeling detached from your surroundings or like you might faint

Chest tightness or a sense that something terrible is about to happen

Emotional and behavioral symptoms can develop as you try to avoid those sensations:

Relying on a friend or family member to accompany you outside

Feeling trapped, frustrated, or ashamed for not being able to “just go out”

Increased anxiety or depression from isolation

Triggers can vary widely, but they usually share one thing: they stir feelings of uncertainty or vulnerability. A crowded concert, a long commute, a sudden noise, or even imagining an unfamiliar situation can spark a fear response.

Crowded or enclosed spaces, like buses, malls, or elevators

Open or exposed places, such as parking lots or wide streets

Previous panic experiences, especially if they happened in public

Health anxiety, such as fearing a medical emergency far from home

Avoidance often feels like relief in the short term, but over time, it reinforces the fear. The brain learns that staying home equals safety, while leaving equals danger.

Agoraphobia can also worsen during periods of high stress or change. Even positive life events—like moving, starting a new job, or entering a relationship—can unsettle a nervous system already wired for hypervigilance.

Recovery focuses on gently retraining your body to tolerate fear without letting it dictate your choices. It's a gradual, compassionate process that rebuilds trust in the world beyond your walls.

Related read: What it actually means to “be triggered” (and how to cope)

When you're living with agoraphobia, recovery can be tricky. You don't want to force yourself to go outside if you don't feel safe. The idea is to build a sense of safety first, starting small and working up to leaving the house. These strategies are drawn from clinical research and real-world practice and are designed to help you move at your own pace while gently retraining your brain and body to trust the world again.

It’s important to remember that avoiding what scares you isn’t a sign of weakness; it’s your brain trying to protect you. Your nervous system probably learned that certain places or situations feel unsafe, so it tries to keep you away.

Agoraphobia sets off a real physiological fear response. When the brain senses threat, it switches on the nervous system's fight-or-flight mode, so your heart rate climbs, your breathing goes shallow, and your muscles tense. Knowing this takes some of the power out of it. You're not going crazy. Your brain is doing its job, in the wrong context.

Start by observing your fear with curiosity. Ask yourself, when does it appear? What sensations come first, what thoughts follow? This kind of mindful attention helps you separate real danger from false alarms. A short daily journal—just a few lines—can make it easier to spot patterns.

💙 If anxiety or panic catches you off guard, reach for Tamara Levitt's Panic SOS session on Calm to work with your breath and body when you need it most.

When panic or anxiety rises, grounding practices can help your body remember it’s safe right now. These techniques calm the stress response by reconnecting you with your senses.

If going outside feels overwhelming, start at home — by an open window or your doorway. Gradually, your body learns that calm is possible beyond your comfort zone.

💙 Try the 5-4-3-2-1 grounding technique on the Calm app.

Gradual exposure therapy—facing feared situations in small, structured steps—is one of the most evidence-based ways to ease agoraphobia. Start where your anxiety feels manageable, then increase the challenge as confidence grows.

Sit near your front door for a few minutes.

Visit a quiet store or café during off-hours.

The aim isn't to feel no anxiety. It's to stay in the situation long enough for anxiety to come down on its own, and to show yourself, again and again, that you can handle it. Each step helps your brain link “outside” with safety. Celebrate even the smallest wins. Progress may be uneven, but every step counts.

💙 Explore Ease Your Social Anxiety with Jeff Warren on Calm, designed to help your world expand again at your own pace.

Avoidance is the mechanism that keeps agoraphobia in place. Every time anxiety pushes you to cancel plans or stay home, and you give in, it reinforces the idea that the feared situation was dangerous. Over time, the list of “unsafe” places and situations tends to grow.

Noticing when avoidance is happening, and gently questioning it, is part of recovery. That doesn't mean forcing yourself into overwhelming situations. It means asking: is this decision based on actual risk, or on anxiety talking?

💙 Turn toward what you're avoiding rather than away from it with Emotions Series: Investigating Anxiety, led by John Armstrong on Calm.

A licensed therapist, especially one trained in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or exposure therapy, can help you challenge anxious thoughts and gradually expand your comfort zone.

If therapy feels intimidating, try starting with a telehealth session. Many people with agoraphobia begin remotely and move to in-person care later. Therapists can also teach tools like cognitive restructuring (questioning catastrophic thoughts) and interoceptive exposure (reducing fear of physical sensations).

If cost is a barrier, ask about low-cost or sliding-scale sessions.

Read more: How CBT can help calm your anxiety (and 5 ways to try it today)

Agoraphobia can feel isolating, but recovery is rarely something you do alone. Support from trusted friends, family, or peer groups can help you stay connected when your world feels small.

Identify one or two people who can listen without minimizing your fear. Be clear about what helps, like “Please don't push me to go out, but check in after I try.”

Online support communities for agoraphobia or panic disorder can also be powerful spaces to share progress and encouragement. Connection doesn't have to mean going far, just not going alone.

Related read: 7 tips on how to communicate your needs in a relationship

Your nervous system can't process new experiences if it's stuck in survival mode. Before trying exposure work, focus on calming your baseline stress.

Slow breathing (inhale 4 counts, exhale 6)

Limiting caffeine or alcohol if they spike anxiety

The longer exhale matters. It activates the parasympathetic nervous system, which helps the body downshift from a high-alert state. These habits won't "cure" agoraphobia, but they can give your body the steadiness it needs to face fear safely.

Mindfulness doesn't mean clearing your mind, but noticing thoughts and sensations without reacting to them. When you can observe fear rather than fight it, it starts to lose its grip.

Then focus on your breath or the feeling of your feet on the floor. You're not trying to make the fear vanish, just reminding yourself you can stay present while it passes. With practice, your brain can learn that fear doesn't always mean danger.

💙 Explore these Tools for Anxiety and Stress with Dr. Julie on the Calm app.

Progress with agoraphobia often feels like two steps forward, one step back. Some days you'll walk outside easily; others, just getting dressed takes effort. That's okay.

Set small, specific goals like opening a window, walking to the mailbox, or standing outside for 30 seconds. Track and celebrate each one. Speak to yourself as you would to a friend since compassion keeps recovery moving when motivation fades.

There will be days when something that felt manageable last week feels impossible again. That's not failure. It's a normal feature of recovering from an anxiety disorder. What matters is returning to your plan after a setback rather than writing off the progress you've made.

Mindfulness won't cure agoraphobia, but it can help you manage it. There's research that suggests mindfulness may reduce anxiety by helping people look at fearful thoughts and body sensations without getting swept up in them.

That matters with agoraphobia. Fear isn't just about the situation you're in. It also sets off a chain of anxious thoughts that make physical symptoms feel worse. Mindfulness helps you notice that chain without automatically following it.

Even five to ten minutes of meditation a day may help change how your brain responds to fear over time. It won't make anxiety go away, but it can make it easier to handle. For anyone who finds leaving home hard, a home-based app like Calm makes this practice easy to access without any extra pressure.

Read more: Mindfulness for beginners: 6 techniques for mindful living

Agoraphobia is treatable. With the right combination of therapy, support, and sometimes medication, many people reclaim a sense of calm and freedom they thought was lost.

Reaching out for help when you can barely leave the house can feel impossible. For many people with agoraphobia, even calling a therapist can trigger anxiety. But asking for help is simply a sign you're ready for support.

Consider professional help if your fear limits work, school, or relationships; if you feel trapped at the thought of leaving home; or if you depend on others to go out. When your world starts shrinking, or hopelessness sets in, it's time for extra care. Early treatment also tends to be more effective than waiting for symptoms to worsen, and it doesn't require hitting a low point first.

Curious to learn more about other phobias and how to treat them?  Having a deeper understanding of common phobias, like acrophobia or metathesiophobia, can help you get to know yourself better and give you tools for treating them or easing their symptoms.

The fear of leaving the house often develops after experiences that made you feel unsafe or out of control — like a panic attack in public, trauma, or chronic stress. Over time, your brain links "outside" with danger and "home" with safety.

Common signs include anxiety or panic outside the home, fear of crowds, public transport, or open and enclosed spaces, and a strong urge to avoid those situations. Some people can only manage them with someone else present. Physical symptoms can include a racing heart, dizziness, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. If this is limiting where you go or what you do, talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

Not always, but they often overlap. Agoraphobia is a clinical term for anxiety about situations where escape might be difficult or help unavailable during panic. The fear of leaving home can be one part of that pattern. Some people feel anxious in only a few situations, while others avoid most public places.

No, though they can overlap. Social anxiety is about fear of judgment from others. Agoraphobia is about fear of situations where escape feels difficult or panic might happen. Both involve avoidance, but the triggers are different and so are the treatment approaches.

Common triggers include crowded or open spaces, traveling alone, driving, public transit, or past experiences of panic. Emotional stress, health worries, or major life changes can also heighten symptoms.

Triggers are deeply personal; learning what sets off your fear is a key part of recovery, because it helps you prepare, plan, and respond with more calm.

Yes. Many people with agoraphobia still leave home but limit when, where, or how they do it — maybe only with a trusted companion or in familiar areas. Agoraphobia exists on a spectrum, and partial avoidance is common.

The goal of treatment isn’t to eliminate all fear, but to help you feel more confident and capable outside, even when anxiety shows up.

Start with very small steps and build gradually. Open the door and stand outside for a minute. Walk to the mailbox. Sit in your car. Over time, extend your distance or duration. Pair these moments with grounding techniques and self-compassion.

If fear or avoidance is getting in the way of work, relationships, or daily life, it's a good time to reach out. You don't need to be housebound to ask for help. A therapist who specializes in anxiety can offer structured treatment, including CBT and exposure work, that's hard to replicate on your own.

Agoraphobia recovery combines understanding, gradual exposure, nervous system regulation, and professional support. Grounding techniques, mindfulness, and therapy—especially cognitive behavioral or exposure therapy—can help retrain your fear response.

Compassion is essential; you’re learning to reintroduce safety to your body, not forcing yourself to be “brave.”

It varies. Some people see real improvement within a few months of consistent CBT and exposure work. Others take a year or more. Progress is usually gradual and setbacks are normal. How long it takes depends on severity, how long symptoms have been present, and access to treatment. Consistency matters more than speed.

Yes, when done properly. Good exposure therapy is gradual. It starts with situations that bring up mild anxiety and builds slowly from there. It should never mean being pushed into something overwhelming without preparation. Working with a trained therapist keeps the pace right and makes sure coping tools are in place before each step.

The most effective treatments are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exposure therapy, and sometimes medication like SSRIs or SNRIs. Teletherapy can also help if in-person sessions feel too difficult.

Many people benefit from combining approaches that balance science with emotional safety.

Yes, when used gently. Meditation can help calm the body’s stress response and increase awareness of anxious thoughts without getting caught in them.

However, for some people, sitting still with intense anxiety can feel overwhelming. Start small—guided breathing, body scans, or walking meditations—and use it as one tool among others, not a cure-all.

Recovery tends to reopen parts of life that anxiety had closed off: work, relationships, travel, and everyday spontaneity. Many people also notice a broader shift in confidence, and find they start attempting things they'd written off, not just outside the home, but in other areas where anxiety had been calling the shots.

Symptoms can lessen over time, especially with self-awareness and stress reduction, but full recovery usually requires intentional support. Without treatment, the avoidance cycle can deepen.

The good news is that with therapy and consistent practice, many people regain independence and confidence, even after years of fear.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9531. How ADHD Science Fails Women in Menopause

Menopause worsens ADHD symptoms, but standard assessments do not capture the depth of women’s misery.

Menopause aggravates and elevates ADHD symptoms for a staggering 97.5 percent of women with the condition, according to a survey of 600 women cited in the Journal of Psychiatric Research.1 Complaints include increased difficulty with attention, emotional regulation, and managing everyday demands – symptoms that significantly degrade quality of life yet remain largely unaddressed in midlife ADHD treatment plans.

The Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale (ASRS) – one of the standard measures for assessing common ADHD symptoms – may not fully capture how much menopause interferes with daily life because it was not specifically designed to measure changes in ADHD across hormonal transitions.

While nearly all of the 600 women in the survey reported worsening ADHD symptoms during menopause, their ASRS scores were similar across different hormonal life stages. This apparent contradiction deserves attention. A woman may experience a major change in mental clarity, working memory, motivation, emotional regulation, and managing day-to-day responsibilities without necessarily showing a large change on a standard ADHD symptom checklist.

[Get This Free Download: Menopause and ADHD]

This points to a critical need for better ways to assess ADHD across the lifespan and to understand how hormonal changes may alter its presentation and impact.

Today, we know about ADHD in menopause thanks, largely, to women’s personal accounts. Though surveys and self-reports cannot establish cause and effect in the same way as controlled clinical trials, they are an essential starting point. They can identify patterns and raise questions that researchers need to investigate.

One central question is regarding the safety and efficacy of prescribing hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and/or ADHD medication to women in perimenopause and menopause. Sadly, evidence specifically supporting combined HRT and stimulant treatment remains limited. We need well-designed studies to determine which women might benefit, what treatments are most effective, and how the medications may interact.

[Read: How Hormonal Changes Impact ADHD Symptoms in Women]

The voices of women with ADHD have brought this issue into view. Now clinicians and researchers have an opportunity – and a responsibility – to listen carefully, investigate rigorously, and translate emerging knowledge into better care.

Kathleen Nadeau, Ph.D., is the founder and clinical director of the Institute for Lifespan ADHD Training.

#9530. Guillaume Cerutti named president of the Palace of Versailles

After eight months without a president, the Palace of Versailles finally has a new leader. Guillaume Cerutti, 60, has been named the president of the prestigious institution, according to the newspaper Politico. A graduate of France’s elite École nationale d’administration (ENA) and a former senior civil servant in the finance ministry, he succeeds Christophe Leribault, who was appointed president and director of the Louvre in February following the abrupt departure of Laurence des Cars.

The appointment marks Cerutti’s return to public service after two decades in the private sector. In a twist of fate, he is following in the footsteps of his former mentor, Jean-Jacques Aillagon, who headed the Palace and National Estate of Versailles from 2007 to 2011. Cerutti worked closely with Aillagon for many years, first at the Centre Pompidou, where Aillagon was the president from 1996 to 2002, and later as his chief of staff when Aillagon became France’s culture minister in 2002. “Having worked alongside Guillaume [Cerutti] for decades, I know he has all the experience and qualities needed to lead Versailles,” Aillagon told Le Monde.

Cerutti went on to put his management skills to work in the art market, becoming head of Sotheby’s France in 2007. In 2015, he was poached by François Pinault, who appointed him president of Christie’s operations in Europe, the Middle East, Russia and India. Just months later, he was promoted to global chief executive of the auction house. At both Sotheby’s and Christie’s, Cerutti built a reputation as a formidable cost-cutter. He also proved adept at steering Christie’s through difficult market conditions.

His next move within the Pinault empire, however, was less successful. In January 2025, Cerutti was appointed president of the Pinault Collection, which oversees the Palazzo Grassi and Punta della Dogana in Venice, as well as the Bourse de Commerce in Paris. Once again, he was following in the footsteps of Aillagon, who had held the same position in the 2010s. But, as Le Monde reports, Cerutti’s efforts to impose the kind of financial discipline he had introduced at Christie’s, coupled with his wish to slow the pace of acquisitions, brought him into conflict with Pinault, who was used to running his collection on his own terms. Barely a year later, Cerutti was forced to step down.

He now assumes one of the most coveted positions in French cultural life, taking charge of a historic palace, museum and gardens that welcomed 8.4 million visitors in 2025 and employ around 1,000 people. His extensive connections in the worlds of business, culture and politics could prove particularly valuable as Versailles faces mounting budgetary pressures and an ever-greater need to secure support from wealthy patrons.

Two decades since the billionaire started planning a home for his collection in the French capital, the spectacular space is due to open on 23 January

The news follows his sudden departure as president of the Pinault Collection

The former chief executive officer of Christie’s moved to Paris to focus on the collection and its museums in 2025

He will be replaced by the president of Christie's America, Bonnie Brennan

#9529. A longer exhale may push your brain toward bolder decisions

A new study suggests that deliberately changing the rhythm of your breathing can influence how you make decisions by altering activity in both the heart and brain. Researchers from the German Institute of Human Nutrition Potsdam-Rehbruecke (DIfE) and Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin found that longer exhalations increased heart rate variability and made the brain more responsive to rewards, which was associated with bolder choices. The findings were published in Neuron.

Fast breathing and an elevated heart rate are often linked with rapid decision-making. Under pressure, people may become more cautious in an effort to avoid losses, whether they are making an investment, handling a tense workplace situation, or choosing a meal quickly. Slower breathing and a calmer cardiovascular state, by contrast, may encourage a more positive assessment of potential outcomes and make people more willing to take risks.

How Breathing Connects the Body and Brain

Decision-making has traditionally been viewed as a process centered mainly in the brain. The new research examined a broader possibility: that signals from other parts of the body can change brain activity and influence the choices people make.

The study was led by Prof. Soyoung Q Park in collaboration with researchers from institutions including the Neuroscience Research Center at Charité -- Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Freie Universität Berlin, and the German Naval Institute of Maritime Medicine.

"Our decisions are rarely determined solely by external information. Rather, our judgment emerges from the interplay between cognitive processes and our current bodily state. It was previously unknown how the conscious regulation of our body, for example through targeted breathing, could actively control our decision-making process. We wanted to create a physiological shift using a slow breathing pattern to change the quality of our decisions," explains Soyoung Q Park, head of the Department of Decision Neuroscience and Nutrition at DIfE, summarizing the research question.

Testing Whether Longer Exhales Change Decisions

The researchers studied 41 healthy participants while they made risky choices under carefully controlled breathing conditions. Participants followed visual breathing instructions and either breathed at their normal individual pace or slowed their breathing while extending the exhalation phase (2:8 inhale-exhale ratio).

As the participants completed a series of risk-related decisions, the research team measured several aspects of their physical and neurological responses. Functional magnetic resonance imaging was used to track brain activity, while breathing patterns, heart activity, skin conductance, and pupil responses were monitored at the same time.

This combination of measurements allowed the researchers to test whether extending the exhale did more than simply lower heart rate. They also wanted to determine whether the breathing pattern directly changed how the brain processed potential rewards.

Longer Exhalation Shifted Choices Toward Reward

The results showed that extended exhalation slowed heart rate and was associated with riskier choices. Importantly, the change appeared to come from greater attention to possible rewards rather than reduced concern about potential losses. Participants still responded to losses in a similar way.

The researchers also detected stronger activity in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the precuneus. These brain regions are involved in reward processing and in regulating the timing between heartbeats, a measure known as heart rate variability.

"Our study thus underscores the transformative role of breath-based interventions. The interplay between breathing and cardiac dynamics makes the brain more receptive to rewards," explains lead author Wenhao Huang, interpreting the results.

What the Findings Could Mean for Breathing Techniques

The work adds to a growing field focused on body-brain communication and supports neurovisceral models, which propose that a person's physical state can strongly shape cognitive processes.

Park explains: "Breathing techniques have accompanied humanity for millennia across various religions and cultures. With this study, we provide scientific proof that it is a reliable and targeted method capable of controlling our decisions."

Because controlled breathing is simple, inexpensive, and relatively easy to learn, the researchers say it could have value as a tool for everyday self-regulation. It may also have potential as a supportive, non-pharmacological approach in clinical settings, particularly for conditions such as anxiety disorders or depression, which can involve disrupted autonomic regulation and altered responses to reward.

Could Breathing Influence Eating Behavior?

Future studies will need to determine whether the same effects appear in broader clinical populations, including people with overweight. The researchers are particularly interested in whether breathing techniques could influence food-related decisions, since eating behavior is strongly affected by both reward processing and a person's physical state.

"Since dietary decisions are strongly influenced by reward assessment and physical state, targeted breath regulation could also play a role in consciously perceiving and more effectively managing eating behavior," Park summarizes for future research activities.

This study was supported by the Federal Ministry for Research, Technology and Space [Grant 01GP2210C (DecEnt-Project), Grant 01EE2301E for the conceptual development of the German Center for Mental Health; Grant 82DZD03D03 (German Center for Diabetes Research)], the Ministry for Science, Research and Culture of the State of Brandenburg (MWFK). Ignacio Rebollo was supported by the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Action (MSCA) BRAINSTOM (grant agreement no. 101028203).

#9527. Calm launches Shift to help people feel better in the moment through sound

Shift is a new dedicated in-app experience designed to help people relieve stress, wind down, focus, and feel better through bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use that moves sound intentionally between your ears.

Shift offers four states to move into, grounded in everyday needs: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep, each through its own custom bilateral track. It also includes a 7-day guided program and 20+ additional tracks to browse, including an exclusive track from popular duo, Daisy the Great.

Shift is one of Calm's largest expansions into a category since Sleep Stories, following increased user and cultural demand since it began developing this content in 2022.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA – October 27, 2026 – Calm, a trusted leader in mental wellness with the #1 app to help you sleep more, stress less and live mindfully, launches Shift – a new in-app offering designed to help people shift how they feel in the moment using bilateral audio, an audio-based approach inspired by a technique therapists use. At launch, Shift provides a 7-day guided program and more than 20 custom bilateral tracks, including an exclusive song by popular New York-based duo, Daisy the Great.

Bilateral audio intentionally moves sound between the left and right ear, creating a natural rhythm designed to help shift your mood, whether that’s finally settling into sleep, releasing the day’s tension, or clearing afternoon fog. No special skills required, just headphones and a few minutes.

Calm added bilateral audio content to its music library in 2022 and has since seen user and cultural demand build. It’s one of the top search terms on Calm, Google search for “bilateral audio” is up over 5000% in the past year, and across the internet, concepts like “brain flossing” have gone viral, pointing to bilateral stimulation to “clear mental clutter”.

“Calm’s origins are rooted in making meditation accessible, but we never intended to be a meditation-only app,” said Dun Wang, CEO of Calm. “We want to be a place people can come to feel better, in whatever way they need. At first it was meditation, then it was sleep, which led to the launch of Sleep Stories, an innovative format that is now one of our most popular offerings. Shift is next, leveraging bilateral sound and music to meet people with approachable, trusted, and deeply human support that leaves them feeling better than when they came.”

7 Days of Shift – a 7-day guided program narrated by Calm meditation teacher Rose Nisker, pairing a few minutes of grounding wisdom with a bilateral track each day.

Shift Your State – 4 new bilateral tracks paired with looping visuals, each composed to shift people into one of four goal states: Focus, Release, Uplift, and Sleep.

Shift Music – an expanded library of new bilateral audio tracks for users to explore any time.

Among the new music is an exclusive bilateral remix of “The Record Player Song” from Daisy the Great. Originally released in 2018, the song became a breakout hit for the duo and has amassed more than 200 million streams across two versions. More recently, Daisy the Great reimagined the track using hocketing, a musical technique in which a single melody is split between two or more voices or instruments, alternating notes and rests, and the new version has gained massive traction across TikTok. It's the first of multiple tracks Calm and Daisy the Great will create together for Shift, continuing Calm’s long-standing approach of partnering with artists to create content that resonates with people.

“We started to make a lot of videos online singing with a technique called hocketing where we split up the melody line and pass it back-and-forth, and it makes a really awesome vocal effect. We did it with our song ‘The Record Player Song,’ and that one really seemed to resonate," said Daisy the Great. "That song already has a bit of a built-in bilateral quality with the melody passing between us, and the overlapping vocals, so it made a lot of sense for Shift. We're so, so excited to be working with Calm and their production team to not only share our music in a new way, but hopefully to help people feel good and connected to themselves too.”

Calm also collaborated with outside consultants certified by the EMDR International Association throughout Shift's development to ensure the content is credible, safe, and suitable for everyday, self-guided use.

“With Shift, Calm takes its already impressive collection of self-soothing programs to another level, thoughtfully integrating guided imagery, relaxing music, and gentle bilateral stimulation,” said Roy Kiessling, LISW. “As an experienced EMDR clinician and trainer, I appreciate the care Calm has taken to emphasize relaxation, emotional comfort, and positive resource enhancement. Shift offers a welcome, accessible way to incorporate soothing bilateral stimulation into everyday emotional well-being.”

#9526. A Parachute for Your ADHD Medication Crash

Most people taking ADHD medication experience an afternoon crash. Here, ADDitude readers reveal effective strategies for a softer landing.

It’s 4 p.m. and your brain is suddenly caught in a riptide. You feel like a swimmer fighting a strong current. The focus, priorities, and momentum that have propelled you forward until now are submerged under a layer of brain fog that rolls in around the same time each day.

This phenomenon is called the ADHD medication crash, and it happens to two-thirds of ADDitude readers who take ADHD medication. When medication levels drop rapidly in the bloodstream, this can result in fatigue, slowed processing speed, and inertia.

According to 3,500 ADDitude survey responses, 57 to 78 percent of stimulant medication users experience a regular crash, with dextroamphetamine and Ritalin LA users reporting the highest prevalence. Even people taking the most popular stimulant medications reported crash prevalence rates of near or above 60 percent. (Users’ experiences with the most popular stimulant medications are shown in the chart below.) The lowest crash prevalence rates were reported by people taking the non-stimulant medications Atomoxetine/Strattera (40%) and guanfacine (52.9%), suggesting that medication crashes are less common with non-stimulant ADHD treatments.

The most common signs of a medication crash, according to ADDitude readers who experience them, include:

The odds of a medication crash increase when an individual is experiencing stress, inadequate sleep, poor diet, and lack of exercise, according to survey respondents. Almost two-thirds of women who experience crashes said their menstrual cycle impacts the crash symptom severity. Readers did not cite medication interactions or caffeine as significant contributors.

The ability to manage household responsibilities is “often” or “always” impaired by medication crashes for 70 percent of survey respondents. Half of crashers say work responsibilities “often” or “always” suffer, and 43 percent say social and family interactions suffer.

#9525. The Urgency of Early ADHD Intervention

Delaying treatment for ADHD until the teen years comes with potential life-long consequences. Here’s what you should know.

Q: I believe my elementary school-age child has ADHD, but my husband doesn’t think so. He refuses to get our child evaluated. I have ADHD and I know this can run in families. What should I do?

This question reflects a dilemma faced by many families: What happens when one parent wants possible signs of ADHD evaluated while another prefers to wait and see? The answer may matter more than many people realize.

Imagine two children entering first grade:

Jacob is bright, curious, and energetic. He struggles to sit still, frequently forgets to turn in his homework, and has difficulty following multi-step instructions. His teacher notices the symptoms and relays these to his parents. Jacob’s pediatrician conducts a comprehensive evaluation and diagnoses Jacob with ADHD.

His parents learn strategies to support him at home. His school implements accommodations. Later, medication becomes part of his treatment plan. Jacob still faces challenges, but he learns how his brain works and develops tools to succeed. He graduates from high school with strong grades and heads off to college.

[Webinar Replay: “6 Principles for Raising a Child with ADHD”]

Now imagine Maya. She is also intelligent, but her suspected ADHD symptoms present differently. She daydreams in class and quietly falls behind. She is emotionally sensitive, often taking criticism to heart and becoming overwhelmed by setbacks that her peers seem to brush off. Her teachers describe her as capable but inconsistent. Because she isn’t disruptive, her struggles are attributed to a lack of effort, disorganization, anxiety, or immaturity.

Year after year, she works harder while feeling increasingly frustrated. As academic demands increase, so do her feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. By the time she receives an ADHD diagnosis at age 16, her grades have suffered, her confidence has eroded, and she is considering leaving school altogether.

The paths of these two children, one who received early intervention with medication and one who remained untreated until her mid-teens, illustrate a growing concern in ADHD care: It’s not simply about whether children are diagnosed, but when.

[Self-Test: Could Your Preschooler Have ADHD?]

A recent study published in JAMA Psychiatry examined educational outcomes among more than 580,000 individuals with ADHD. The researchers found that children diagnosed earlier in life had significantly better educational outcomes than those diagnosed during adolescence. Earlier diagnosis with associated with higher grade point averages, a greater likelihood of pursuing academic educational tracks, and substantially lower rates of school dropout.

The differences were striking. Individuals diagnosed during the early elementary school years had school dropout rates of approximately 9 percent by age 20, compared with nearly 30 percent among those first diagnosed around age 16. Similar patterns were observed in both males and females. The researchers concluded that adolescents diagnosed later represent a particularly vulnerable group.

The findings do not suggest that a diagnosis alone changes a child’s future. Rather, earlier recognition creates opportunities for intervention. Children identified sooner can access school accommodations, behavioral supports, parent education, and, when appropriate, medication – before years of academic struggles, self-doubt, and declining confidence take hold and begin to shape their identity.

This raises an important question: How many Mayas are sitting in classrooms today, struggling silently while waiting years for recognition or a diagnosis?

Universal ADHD screening offers a potential solution. Many children with ADHD are identified only after academic, social, or emotional difficulties have become impossible to ignore. Screening creates an opportunity to recognize concerns earlier before the consequences of undiagnosed ADHD begin to accumulate. Importantly, screening is not diagnosis. It is simply an invitation to look more closely.

Many critics of universal screening worry about overdiagnosis or unnecessary labeling. Those concerns deserve consideration. However, screening itself does not determine whether a child has ADHD. It merely identifies children who may benefit from a more comprehensive evaluation, meaning that fewer children with significant challenges get overlooked.

Growing evidence suggests that every year of delayed recognition carries educational and emotional costs that are difficult to reverse. Universal screening will not identify every child. But it may help more children find the right path before they wander too far afield.

For many children, the greatest risk may not be receiving an ADHD diagnosis. It may be never receiving one at all.

#9524. Is sharenting safe? 7 ways to mindfully post about your kids online

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your kid loses their first tooth or says something hilarious at dinner, and your thumb is already halfway to the share button. For a lot of parents and caregivers, posting these moments feels like second nature.

Believe it or not, there's actually a name for this habit: sharenting. And while it’s often a simple way to stay connected, it also puts your child’s story online before they can choose to share it. If you’ve started to wonder about the risks, it’s a good time to take stock of your posting habits.

Here's a look at why parents share and what’s worth knowing about the risks, plus seven small shifts to help you post with confidence.

Sharenting is when parents or caregivers post about their kids on social media. It could be a single birthday photo, or years of posts documenting a whole childhood. Think videos, funny quotes, school updates, potty-training wins, and even ultrasound pictures from before the baby arrives.

It's also widespread. Research reviews estimate that about three in four parents share photos, stories, or videos of their kids online, and most use their children's real names.

Parents have always shared news about their kids through holiday letters, birth announcements, and photos mailed to relatives. Social media just made the audience much bigger, the posts more public, and the record harder to remove.

Most sharenting comes from a good place. You're proud of your kid and you want the people in your life to know. Studies on parents who post about their kids point to the same reasons:

Staying close: Photos and videos let faraway family and friends watch your child grow.

Celebrating and remembering: Posts mark your child’s milestones and give you something to scroll back through later.

Finding community: Other parents and caregivers can offer advice and a “me too” at 2am, when parenting feels isolating.

Feeling seen: A kind comment on a rough day reminds you that you’re doing okay.

💙 Feeling alone as a parent? Here’s how to deal with loneliness.

Sharing your kids online isn’t necessarily harmful. Still, a few risks are worth knowing about:

A lasting digital footprint. Screenshots, reshares, and archives mean a photo can outlast the original post. Many kids have years of photos online before they're old enough to understand who can see them.

Personal information. Someone could piece together a full name, birth date, hometown, and school from a handful of posts. Over time, details like these may be misused for identity theft.

Location and background details. Location tags and details like a house number, school logo, or regular park in the background show where your child spends their time. On a public account, that can make their routine visible to strangers.

Facial recognition and AI. Photos on public accounts may be saved, scanned, or collected by AI tools and facial recognition software. Some of those tools turn ordinary photos into fake images.

💙 Want to bring more intention to parenting, online and off? Start here.

Before you hit share, take a breath and think about whether you want to post this moment. If you do, scan the photo and caption for anything that gives away too much, like a full name or a street sign.

For some structure, a short breathing exercise or meditation can help.

💙 Listen to Pause to Breathe with Prof. Megan Reitz on Calm.

A couple of settings are worth checking before your next post. If your account is public, anyone can find and save your posts. Photos taken on your phone may also include the location where you took them.

Switch to a private account and remove followers you don’t know.

Turn off geotagging in your camera and app settings.

Platforms can change their defaults without warning, so it’s worth redoing this check every couple of months.

You can share the moment without giving away your child’s identity. Skip birth dates, school names, and daily routines. Use a nickname or first initial instead of your child’s full name.

Posting a day or two later makes it harder for anyone to know where your child is in real time.

Once your child is old enough to weigh in, show them the post and ask if they're okay with you sharing it. This shows them that their opinion matters. If your child is too young to decide, the next tip can help you decide for them.

Imagine your child at 25, seeing what you’re about to post. Does it give away something private about them, such as a health issue or a hard time at school? What seems relatable now may feel too personal to them later.

If you're unsure, keep the more personal moments in a private family group or an offline album.

💙 Explore Shift Your Perspective with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your past posts felt right at the time, and it’s okay if some show more than you’d share today. Scroll back through your posts for details like full names, school names, or locations.

Delete the post, archive it, or move it to a private album if it feels too revealing.

You're not the only one with a camera. Grandparents, co-parents, babysitters, and friends may post photos of your child too, usually out of love and pride. A conversation up front about family boundaries keeps everyone on the same page.

leave full names and birth dates out of captions

skip location tags and recognizable landmarks in the background

use private groups or shared albums instead of public posts

💙 Calm’s Kind Communication session can help you find the words for a warm, open conversation.

Sharenting means posting about your child on social media, and the word blends "sharing" and "parenting." It covers anything from baby photos to regular updates as they grow up.

Common sharenting examples include ultrasound pictures, birthday posts, funny quotes, and health or milestone updates. Even a photo that seems harmless can reveal more than you intended, like a club sign or a team jersey in the background.

Many parents share to stay connected and celebrate their kids. Sharenting keeps faraway family members in the loop and connects you with other parents who get it. During hard stretches, it can help you feel less alone.

The main risks of sharenting include a lasting digital footprint and exposed personal details. Photos can be saved, reshared, or collected by AI tools, which is why child safety groups encourage private accounts.

That said, many posts don’t lead to harm, and small habits like turning off location tags help lower the risks further.

Sharenting shapes your child’s public image before they’re old enough to agree to it. Names, schools, and tagged locations can also reveal their routines to strangers, and a handful of details may be used for identity theft.

If you keep personal moments offline now, your child has more room to shape their own image as they grow.

There's no set age for when kids should have a say in what you post. Young kids may not fully understand what sharing means, so the decision starts with you. You can start asking as soon as they’re able to weigh in, and give their yes or no more weight as they grow.

#9523. Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome

Researchers at Carnegie Mellon University's School of Computer Science, the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine and the University of Washington have uncovered a previously underexplored feature of Alzheimer's disease that may help scientists identify new avenues for treatment.

The study, published in Science, found that the three-dimensional organization of the genome differs in certain brain cells from people with Alzheimer's disease. Scientists from SCS's Ray and Stephanie Lane Computational Biology Department, Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, and collaborating institutions connected these changes in genome folding with shifts in gene activity and the organization of brain tissue.

To build this detailed picture, the team combined single-cell technology, spatial mapping of brain tissue, and a newly developed deep learning model.

"Alzheimer's disease cannot be understood one layer at a time," said Jian Ma, the Ray and Stephanie Lane Professor of Computational Biology who led and supervised the study. "The genome's 3D structure is a fundamental regulatory layer that helps to connect DNA sequence to gene activity. By integrating genome folding, cell state, and tissue context, we can move beyond cataloging disease-associated changes toward understanding how they fit together and which mechanisms to test next."

DNA does not sit inside a cell as a simple straight strand. Instead, it folds into a complex three-dimensional structure that helps determine which genes are accessible and active. Changes in that physical organization can therefore influence how cells function.

The researchers examined postmortem samples from the prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain. The tissue came from people with and without Alzheimer's disease who had taken part in a long-term dementia study and later donated their brains for research.

The team used GAGE-seq, a technique that can measure both gene expression and three-dimensional genome contacts within the same individual cell. Those measurements were then combined with spatial transcriptomic maps, which preserve information about where gene activity occurs within intact brain tissue.

By bringing these datasets together, the researchers were able to connect the physical organization of the genome with gene regulation while also seeing where Alzheimer's related molecular and cellular changes appeared within the surrounding tissue.

"Our study represents a major advance in understanding what goes wrong in Alzheimer's disease," said Hansruedi Mathys, assistant professor of neurobiology at Pitt's Department of Neurobiology, who directed the Pitt arm of the study. "We know the classic hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease - accumulation of amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles - but our results establish higher-order chromatin alterations as a component of the molecular pathology associated with the disease, which currently affects seven million Americans, a number that continues to grow."

Amyloid beta plaques and tau tangles are among the best known biological features of Alzheimer's disease. The new findings suggest that changes in chromatin, the material made of DNA and associated proteins that packages the genome inside cells, should also be considered part of the disease's molecular landscape.

AI Connects Genome Folding to Gene Activity

Another important part of the research was Hicformer, an artificial intelligence model developed to investigate how genome structure may influence cellular behavior. The model combines DNA sequence information with broad patterns of genome folding and detailed maps showing where different sections of DNA physically contact one another.

Using these inputs, Hicformer predicts gene activity across different types of cells. Xinyue Lu, a doctoral student in Computational Biology who co-led the research, described the system as a computational test bed that can be used to explore how changes in genome folding might alter gene activity.

"Measuring gene activity and genome folding in the same cell allows us to directly connect chromosome structure with disease-related gene programs," said Yang Zhang, a project scientist in the Computational Biology Department who co-led the research. "Across several kinds of brain cells, this paired view revealed a consistent signature of 3D genome reorganization in Alzheimer's disease and helped us prioritize regulatory regions for future mechanistic and therapeutic investigation."

The researchers identified several consistent differences in the genome architecture of cells from people with Alzheimer's disease.

Large sections of the genome are normally organized into relatively distinct active and inactive regions known as compartments. In Alzheimer's cells, those boundaries appeared less sharply defined. The researchers describe this pattern as "increased compartment mingling."

Several kinds of brain cells also showed fewer interactions between nearby sections of the genome and more contacts between regions located farther apart. Cells with greater compartment mingling tended to have lower overall levels of gene activity.

The team also observed weaker interactions between genes and nearby regulatory elements that normally help control whether those genes are switched on or off. At the same time, some contacts across intermediate distances became stronger.

These structural differences were associated with reduced activity in programs involved in neurons and synapses, along with changes in metabolism and cellular stress responses. The researchers also found links to senescence-related programs in microglia, immune cells in the brain that play important roles in maintaining brain health and responding to damage.

Potential Clues for Future Alzheimer's Treatments

When the researchers mapped these molecular changes across intact brain tissue, they found that the reorganization of the genome was connected not only to altered gene activity but also to differences in how brain cells were arranged within the tissue.

The results establish three-dimensional genome organization as another important layer of Alzheimer's disease biology. They also provide researchers with a framework for testing which changes in genome architecture might directly contribute to the disease.

Future studies can now investigate whether particular structural changes help drive Alzheimer's progression and whether any of the affected regulatory regions could eventually become targets for new therapies.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health. Other CMU authors included doctoral students Shahul Alam and Shike Wang and postdoctoral research associate Junjie Tang. Other Pitt authors include doctoral students Alexander K. Kunisky and Jude Baroudi, post-baccalaureate research fellows Sahar and Sahel Ghorbanikalateh, and visiting scholar Shihan Wang. The team included researchers from the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Washington; and the Rush Alzheimer's Disease Center.

Materials provided by University of Pittsburgh. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#9521. Art Collaboration Kyoto fair celebrates six years of matchmaking galleries

The sixth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto includes 52 galleries in the main section and 11 galleries in the Kyoto Meetings section Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

This year marks the sixth edition of Art Collaboration Kyoto (ACK), the fair that pairs Japanese commercial galleries with international peers to collaborate on shared stands. The fair will take place from 7 to 9 November at the Kyoto International Conference Center. The event has become known for its distinctive exhibitor model, which has proved popular with exhibitors and fair attendees alike.

“We thought, ‘If we are going to do this, why not create a fair that galleries and artists themselves would find exciting and genuinely want to be part of?’” Miho Doi, ACK’s director of experiences, tells The Art Newspaper about the fair’s founding.

This year’s edition includes a number of high-profile Western galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Jeffrey Deitch and Carlos Ishikawa, alongside Asian galleries such as Seoul’s Gallery Hyundai.

The collaborative format is intended to give both Japanese and international galleries an opportunity to work together and introduce their artists and programmes to new audiences. Pairing domestic and foreign galleries has been key for the success of the fair, organisers say, especially for dealers without experience in Japan.

“For an overseas gallery, participating independently in an art fair in a country it is entering for the first time is by no means easy,” Doi says. “We have heard from participating galleries that, for a variety of reasons, taking part in a Japanese fair entirely on their own would not have been realistic.”

The fair’s main section will bring together 52 galleries. Taro Nasu from Tokyo will join forces with Hauser & Wirth for a presentation focused on text in contemporary art, including works by Louise Bourgeois, Jenny Holzer, David Horvitz and Glenn Ligon, among others. Nanzuka from Tokyo will work alongside Jeffrey Deitch, while Tokyo Gallery + BTAP will team up with Gallery Hyundai for a presentation pairing post-war Japanese and Korean experimental practices, including the Korean artist Seung-taek Lee in dialogue with the Japanese artist Kishio Suga.

“Some participating galleries have even described ACK as a ‘fair built on friendship’ rather than a place for competition,” Doi says.

Another section of the fair is dedicated to presentations from 11 individual galleries with strong connections to Kyoto. Mendes Wood DM, for instance, will present works by Tomie Ohtake—who was born in Kyoto and later relocated to São Paulo, which is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan—among other artists. Hong Kong’s Kiang Malingue will show works by Yang Chi-Chuan and Faye Wei Wei, whose sculptures and paintings respond to Kyoto’s landscapes and urban environment.

A joint stand with Nonaka-Hill and Hoffman Donahue galleries Courtesy Art Collaboration Kyoto

The fair also coincides with a programme of special exhibitions and projects across Kyoto. This year, the Scottish painter Andrew Cranston will present an installation at Ryosokuin Temple, a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto’s historic Gion district. The exhibition is organised by Modern Art and Ingleby. Elsewhere, Carlos Ishikawa will stage a presentation of work by Evelyn Taocheng Wang and Issy Wood at Korin-in Temple.

This edition of ACK takes place under a new leadership committee structure, introduced earlier this year. Rather than being led by a single fair director, ACK is now guided by a seven-member committee with expertise spanning art consulting, cultural foundations, Kyoto cultural policy, fair production, education, partnerships and collector relations. The former fair director, Yukako Yamashita, now leads the fair’s ambassador programme.

As for ACK’s next six years, Doi says the leadership committee aims to develop the fair into a platform that “connects the art scenes of Japan and the world and generates a virtuous cycle between cultural and commercial value”.

#9519. Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks

Scientists at the Mark and Mary Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute (Stevens INI) at the Keck School of Medicine of USC have uncovered evidence that two neighboring types of brain tissue may work together to support thinking abilities later in life. Their findings suggest that the condition of the brain's local communication pathways could influence how strongly gray matter loss affects cognition.

The study, published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association, included brain imaging and cognitive testing from 459 adults aged 60 and older living in communities across India. The research is among the first to investigate superficial white matter in a community-based population from a low- and middle-income country.

Superficial white matter forms a thin layer of nerve fibers directly beneath the gray matter covering the outside of the brain. These short, curved fibers connect nearby regions of the cerebral cortex, allowing them to exchange information. They can be thought of as local roads linking neighboring areas of the brain.

Gray matter serves a different role. It contains many of the nerve cells responsible for processing information. Together, gray matter and the white matter directly beneath it form closely connected systems that may both contribute to cognitive health.

"Gray matter and superficial white matter are physically close and may play different roles: gray matter processes information, while superficial white matter helps nearby brain regions communicate," said Yingxu Liu, PhD, a postdoctoral scholar at the Stevens INI and first author of the study. "Our findings suggest that cognitive health depends not only on how much gray matter is preserved, but also on the condition of the wiring that connects it."

To investigate these local connections, the researchers used an advanced type of diffusion MRI. This imaging technique tracks the movement of water through brain tissue, allowing scientists to examine microscopic features that conventional brain scans may not reveal.

The researchers focused on measurements related to neurite density and the amount of freely moving water surrounding these structures. Neurites are the small projections through which nerve cells send and receive signals. A lower density of neurites or an increase in free water can indicate damage or disruption in tissue associated with processes including loss of myelin, inflammation, or swelling.

Participants also underwent assessments covering several areas of cognition, including language, memory, executive function, and visuospatial ability.

The most consistent connection between superficial white matter health and cognitive performance involved language. People with healthier superficial white matter tended to perform better on language tests. The strongest associations appeared in frontotemporal regions of the brain involved in recognizing words, speaking fluently, and temporarily holding language information in mind.

Healthy Wiring May Cushion Gray Matter Loss

Measures of gray matter atrophy were still the strongest overall predictors of cognitive ability. However, the researchers found that the impact of gray matter loss appeared to vary depending on the health of nearby superficial white matter.

When these local connections showed poorer integrity, gray matter loss was more strongly associated with impaired language performance and broader cognitive difficulties. When superficial white matter was healthier, the link between gray matter loss and poorer cognition was weaker.

This raises the possibility that the condition of the brain's local wiring could help explain why two people with similar amounts of gray matter loss do not necessarily experience the same degree of cognitive decline.

"The findings point to superficial white matter as a possible source of resilience," said Leon Aksman, PhD, assistant professor of research neurology at the Stevens INI and senior author of the study. "Two people with a similar degree of gray matter loss may not experience the same cognitive effects if the local connections surrounding that gray matter differ in health. Following participants over time will be essential to test whether preserving these connections can help maintain cognition."

Expanding Brain Aging Research Beyond Typical Populations

The researchers drew their data from the Harmonized Diagnostic Assessment of Dementia for the Longitudinal Aging Study in India, known as LASI-DAD. More than half of the larger LASI-DAD population has low literacy, while about 60% lives in rural communities.

Populations with these characteristics have historically been underrepresented in brain imaging studies, making the research an opportunity to examine cognitive aging across a broader range of social, educational, and geographic backgrounds.

In this analysis, the association between superficial white matter and language ability was stronger among people who were unable to read or who read incorrectly, those who had received no formal education, and participants living in rural areas.

The researchers emphasize that the results do not establish that these social factors caused changes in brain tissue. Instead, they suggest that brain aging may be shaped by a complex combination of experiences throughout life, including education, social circumstances, health, and environmental exposures.

Because participants were examined at only one point in time, the study cannot establish which brain changes occurred first. Researchers do not yet know whether deterioration of superficial white matter begins before gray matter loss, develops alongside it, or precedes measurable cognitive decline.

Long-term research that follows people as they age will be needed to clarify these relationships. Future studies will also investigate how vascular health, inflammation, Alzheimer's related proteins, and other biological factors interact with changes in gray and white matter.

"A fuller understanding of brain aging requires research that reflects the world's social, cultural, and geographic diversity," said Arthur W. Toga, PhD, director of the Stevens INI and Provost Professor at USC. "By studying an underrepresented population and looking beyond gray matter alone, this work brings us closer to identifying the biological and social factors that may protect cognition across the lifespan."

In addition to Liu and Aksman, the study's authors include Kirsten M. Lynch, Miguel Arce Rentería, Emma Nichols, Alden L. Gross, Lindsay C. Kobayashi, Neda Jahanshad, John P. John, Harshita V.
